section.heading: Conservation of Energy
section.paragraph: Let’s apply the ideas of this chapter to a continuous force field $$\mathbf{F}$$ that moves an object along a path $$C$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}{(t)}$$ , $$a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$ , where $$\mathbf{r}{(a)} = A$$ is the initial point and $$\mathbf{r}{(b)} = B$$ is the terminal point of $$C$$ . According to Newton’s Second Law of Motion (see Section 13.4), the force $$\mathbf{F}{({\mathbf{r}{(t)}})}$$ at a point on $$C$$ is related to the acceleration $$\mathbf{a}{(t)} = \mathbf{r}^{''}{(t)}$$ by the equation
$$\mathbf{F}{({\mathbf{r}{(t)}})} = m\mathbf{r}^{''}{(t)}$$
So the work done by the force on the object is
Therefore
$$W = \frac{1}{2}m\left| {\mathbf{v}{(b)}} \right|^{2} - \frac{1}{2}m\left| {\mathbf{v}{(a)}} \right|^{2}$$
where $$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{r}^{\prime}$$ is the velocity.

The quantity $$\frac{1}{2}m\left| {\mathbf{v}{(t)}} \right|^{2}$$ , that is, half the mass times the square of the speed, is called the kinetic energy of the object. Therefore we can rewrite Equation 15 as
which says that the work done by the force field along $$C$$ is equal to the change in kinetic energy at the endpoints of $$C$$ .

Now let’s further assume that $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a conservative force field; that is, we can write $$\mathbf{F} = \nabla f$$ . In physics, the potential energy of an object at the point $$({x,y,z})$$ is defined as $$P{({x,y,z})} = - f{({x,y,z})}$$ , so we have $$\mathbf{F} = - \nabla P$$ . Then by Theorem 2 we have
$$W = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = - {\int_{C}{\nabla P \cdot d\mathbf{r}}}}} = - \left\lbrack {P{({\mathbf{r}{(b)}})} - P{({\mathbf{r}{(a)}})}} \right\rbrack = P{(A)} - P{(B)}$$
Comparing this equation with Equation 16, we see that

which says that if an object moves from one point $$A$$ to another point $$B$$ under the influence of a conservative force field, then the sum of its potential energy and its kinetic energy remains constant. This is called the Law of Conservation of Energy and it is the reason the vector field is called conservative.

$$C:\mathbf{r}{(t)} = \sin t\mathbf{i} + t\mathbf{j} + 2t\mathbf{k},0 \leqslant t \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$

problem.paragraph: Inverse Square Fields Suppose that $$\mathbf{F}$$ is an inverse square force field, that is,
$$\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{c\mathbf{r}}{\left| \mathbf{r} \right|^{3}}$$
for some constant $$c$$ , where $$\mathbf{r} = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + z\mathbf{k}$$ .

list.item: Find the work done by $$\mathbf{F}$$ in moving an object from a point $$P_{1}$$ along a path to a point $$P_{2}$$ in terms of the distances $$d_{1}$$ and $$d_{2}$$ from these points to the origin.

An example of an inverse square field is the gravitational field $$\mathbf{F} = - {({mMG})}r \slash |r|^{3}$$ discussed in Example 16.1.4. Use part (a) to find the work done by the gravitational field when the earth moves from aphelion (at a maximum distance of $$1.52 \times 10^{8}$$ km from the sun) to perihelion (at a minimum distance of $$1.47 \times 10^{8}$$ km). section.heading: 16.4. Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: Green’s Theorem gives the relationship between a line integral around a simple closed curve and a double integral over the plane region bounded by the curve.
section.heading: Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: Let $$C$$ be a simple closed curve and let $$D$$ be the region bounded by $$C$$ , as in Figure 1. (We assume that $$D$$ consists of all points inside $$C$$ as well as all points on $$C$$ .) In stating Green’s Theorem we use the convention that the positive orientation of a simple closed curve $$C$$ refers to a single counterclockwise traversal of $$C$$ . Thus if $$C$$ is given by the vector function $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ , $$a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$ , then the region $$D$$ is always on the left as the point $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ traverses $$C$$ . (See Figure 2.)

The closed curve labeled C, is larger on the right and a bit narrow on the left and has a small upward bump at the bottom left. An arrowhead placed on the curve points anticlockwise. The region within the curve is shaded and labeled D.

The curve, labeled C, is an irregular closed curve with three fingers protruding upward and one finger protruding downward. The arrowheads on the curve point counterclockwise. The region within the curve is shaded and labeled D. An irregular closed curve and a shaded region are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The arrowheads on the curve point clockwise. The region within the curve is shaded and labeled D.

note.title: Green’s Theorem
note.heading: Green’s Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$C$$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane and let $$D$$ be the region bounded by $$C$$ . If $$P$$ and $$Q$$ have continuous partial derivatives on an open region that contains $$D$$ , then
$$\int_{C}Pdx + Qdy = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}$$

section.paragraph: Recall that the left side of this equation is another way of writing $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ , where $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}$$ .
Note The notation
$$\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}$$
or
$$\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}$$

is sometimes used to indicate that the line integral is calculated using the positive orientation of the closed curve $$C$$ . Another notation for the positively oriented boundary curve of $$D$$ is $$\partial D$$ , so the equation in Green’s Theorem can be written as
$$\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\int_{\partial D}{Pdx + Qdy}}}$$

Green’s Theorem should be regarded as the counterpart of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for double integrals. Compare Equation 1 with the statement of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2, in the following equation:
$$\int_{a}^{b}{F^{\prime}(x)dx = F(b) - F(a)}$$

In both cases there is an integral involving derivatives ( $$F^{\prime}$$ , $$\partial Q \slash \partial x$$ , and $$\partial P \slash \partial y$$ ) on the left side of the equation. And in both cases the right side involves the values of the original functions ( $$F$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$P$$ ) only on the boundary of the domain. (In the one-dimensional case, the domain is an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ whose boundary consists of just two points, $$a$$ and $$b$$ .)
Green’s Theorem is not easy to prove in general, but we can give a proof for the special case where the region is both type I and type II (see Section 15.2). Let’s call such regions simple regions.

note.source_type: Proof of Green’s Theorem for the Case in Which D Is a Simple Region
note.title: Proof of Green’s Theorem for the Case in Which D Is a Simple Region
note.heading: Proof of Green’s Theorem for the Case in Which D Is a Simple Region
note.paragraph: Notice that Green’s Theorem will be proved if we can show that
$$\int_{C}{Pdx = - {\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dA}}}$$
and
$$\int_{C}{Qdy = {\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}dA}}}$$
We prove Equation 2 by expressing $$D$$ as a type I region:
$$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| a \leqslant x \leqslant b,g_{1}(x) \leqslant y \leqslant g_{2}(x) \right\}$$
where $$g_{1}$$ and $$g_{2}$$ are continuous functions. This enables us to compute the double integral on the right side of Equation 2 as follows:

$${\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dA = {\int_{a}^{b}{\int_{g_{1}(x)}^{g_{2}(x)}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\left( {x,y} \right)dydx}}}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {P\left( {x,g_{2}(x)} \right) - P\left( {x,g_{1}(x)} \right)} \right\rbrack dx}}$$
where the last step follows from the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

Now we compute the left side of Equation 2 by breaking up $$C$$ as the union of the four curves $$C_{1}$$ , $$C_{2}$$ , $$C_{3}$$ , and $$C_{4}$$ shown in Figure 3. On $$C_{1}$$ we take $$x$$ as the parameter and write the parametric equations as $$x = x$$ , $$y = g_{1}(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Thus
$$\int_{C_{1}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = {\int_{a}^{b}{P\left( {x,g_{1}(x)} \right)dx}}}$$

Observe that $$C_{3}$$ goes from right to left but $$- C_{3}$$ goes from left to right, so we can write the parametric equations of $$- C_{3}$$ as $$x = x$$ , $$y = g_{2}(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ . Therefore
$$\int_{C_{3}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\int_{- C_{3}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\int_{a}^{b}{P\left( {x,g_{2}(x)} \right)dx}}}}}$$
On $$C_{2}$$ or $$C_{4}$$ (either of which might reduce to just a single point), $$x$$ is constant, so $$dx = 0$$ and
$$\int_{C_{2}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = 0 = {\int_{C_{4}}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx}}}$$
Hence

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}P(x,y)dx} = {\int_{C_{1}}P(x,y)dx + \int_{C_{2}}P(x,y)dx + \int_{C_{3}}P(x,y)dx + \int_{C_{4}}P(x,y)dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}P(x,y)dx} = {\int_{a}^{b}P\left( {x,g_{1}(x)} \right)dx - \int_{a}^{b}P\left( {x,g_{2}(x)} \right)dx}} \end{array}$$
Comparing this expression with the one in Equation 4, we see that
$$\int_{C}{P\left( {x,y} \right)dx = - {\iint\limits_{D}{\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}dA}}}$$
Equation 3 can be proved in much the same way by expressing $$D$$ as a type II region (see Exercise 34). Then, by adding Equations 2 and 3, we obtain Green’s Theorem.

image.alt: Details A four-part closed curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x-axis has two tick marks: a and b, with a to the left of b. The first curve, labeled C_1, defined by y = g_1(x), begins from directly above a, briefly goes down to the right, concaves up, reaches a low point, and then goes up to the right, concaves down until directly above b. The second part of the curve, labeled c_2, briefly runs vertically upward. The third part of the curve, labeled c_3 and defined by y = g_2(x), is a reflection of C_1. It begins from the endpoint of C_2, directly above b, goes up to the right, initially concave up and then concave down, reaches a high point, briefly goes down to the right, concave down. The fourth part of the curve, labeled C_4, runs vertically downward directly above a, to meet the starting point of C_1 and is longer than C_2. The region within the four-part closed curve is labeled D.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int_{C}{x^{4}dx + xydy}}_{}$$ , where $$C$$ is the triangular curve consisting of the line segments from $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ , from $$\left( {1,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ , and from $$\left( {0,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ .

Solution Although the given line integral could be evaluated as usual by the methods of Section 16.2, that would involve setting up three separate integrals along the three sides of the triangle, so let’s use Green’s Theorem instead. Notice that the region $$D$$ enclosed by $$C$$ is simple and $$C$$ has positive orientation (see Figure 4). If we let $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{4}$$ and $$Q\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ , then we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}x^{4}dx + xydy = \iint\limits_{D}\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA} = {\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{1 - x}(y - 0)dydx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}x^{4}dx + xydy} = {\int_{0}^{1}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}y^{2}} \right\rbrack_{y = 0}^{y = 1 - x}dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}{(1 - x)}^{2}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}x^{4}dx + xydy}{= - \frac{1}{6}{(1 - x)}^{3}\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{6}}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A triangular curve and a shaded region are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The triangular curve has its vertices at (0, 0), (1, 0), and (0, 1). An arrowhead is placed on each side of the triangle and points counterclockwise. The hypotenuse of the triangle is labeled y = 1 minus x). The region within the curve is shaded and labeled D.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\oint_{C}{{({3y - e^{\sin x}})}dx}} + \left( {7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}} \right)dy$$ , where $$C$$ is the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ .
Solution The region $$D$$ bounded by $$C$$ is the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 9$$ , so let’s change to polar coordinates after applying Green’s Theorem:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\oint_{C}{(3y - e^{\sin x})}^{}dx} + {\left( {7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}} \right)dy} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}} \right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}{({3y - e^{\sin x}})}} \right\rbrack dA}} \\ {\phantom{{\oint_{C}{(3y - e^{\sin x})}^{}dx} + {{({7x + \sqrt{y^{4} + 1}})}dy}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{3}(7 - 3)rdrd\theta = 4\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\theta\int_{0}^{3}rdr = 36\pi}} \end{array}$$
Instead of using polar coordinates, we could simply use the fact that $$D$$ is a disk of radius $$3$$ and write
$$\iint\limits_{D}4dA = 4 \cdot \pi(3)^{2} = 36\pi$$

section.paragraph: In Examples 1 and 2 we found that the double integral was easier to evaluate than the line integral. (Try setting up the line integral in Example 2 and you’ll soon be convinced!) But sometimes it’s easier to evaluate the line integral, and Green’s Theorem is used in the reverse direction. For instance, if it is known that $$P\left( {x,y} \right) = Q\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ on the curve $$C$$ , then Green’s Theorem gives
$$\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy = 0}}}$$
no matter what values $$P$$ and $$Q$$ assume in the region $$D$$ .
section.heading: Finding Areas with Green's Theorem
section.paragraph: Another application of the reverse direction of Green’s Theorem is in computing areas. Since the area of $$D$$ is $$\iint_{D}{1dA}$$ , we wish to choose $$P$$ and $$Q$$ so that
$$\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 1$$
There are several possibilities:
$$\begin{array}{lll} {P(x,y) = 0} & { P(x,y) = - y} & { P(x,y) = - \frac{1}{2}y} \\ {Q(x,y) = x} & { Q(x,y) = 0} & { Q(x,y) = \frac{1}{2}x} \end{array}$$
Then Green’s Theorem gives the following formulas for the area of $$D$$ :
$$A = {\oint_{C}{xdy = - {\oint_{C}{ydx = \frac{1}{2}{\oint_{C}{xdy - ydx}}}}}}$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the area enclosed by the ellipse $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1$$ .
Solution The ellipse has parametric equations $$x = a\cos t$$ and $$y = b\sin t$$ , where $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Using the third formula in Equation 5, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\frac{1}{2}\int_{C}xdy - ydx}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}(a\cos t)(b\cos t)dt - (b\sin t)( - a\sin t)dt}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\frac{ab}{2}\int_{0}^{2\pi}dt = \pi ab}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Formula 5 can be used to explain how planimeters work. A planimeter is an ingenious mechanical instrument invented in the 19th century for measuring the area of a region by tracing its boundary curve. For instance, a biologist could use one of these devices to measure the surface area of a leaf or bird wing.

Figure 5 shows the operation of a polar planimeter: the pole is fixed and, as the tracer is moved along the boundary curve of the region, the wheel partly slides and partly rolls perpendicular to the tracer arm. The planimeter measures the distance that the wheel rolls and this is proportional to the area of the enclosed region. The explanation as a consequence of Formula 5 can be found in the following articles:

list.item: R. W. Gatterman, “The planimeter as an example of Green’s Theorem” Amer. Math. Monthly, Vol. 88 (1981), pp. 701–4.
Tanya Leise, “As the planimeter wheel turns” College Math. Journal, Vol. 38 (2007), pp. 24–31.

image.alt: Details The figure shows a planimeter and a simple closed curve. Arrowheads placed on the curve point clockwise. The planimeter has a tracer that touches the curve and is connected to a beam labeled tracer arm on top. The tracer arm is connected to the front right corner of a rectangular frame. The left side of the frame has two wheels touching each other: one rotates left and right and the other rotate front and back. The top right corner of the frame is labeled pivot and is connected to the left end of a rod labeled polearm with a short cylinder labeled pole at its right end.

figure.caption: A Keuffel and Esser polar planimeter

note.title: George Green
note.heading: George Green
note.paragraph: Green’s Theorem is named after the self-taught English scientist George Green (1793–1841). He worked full-time in his father’s bakery from the age of nine and taught himself mathematics from library books. In 1828 he published privately An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism, but only $$100$$ copies were printed and most of those went to his friends. This pamphlet contained a theorem that is equivalent to what we know as Green’s Theorem, but it didn’t become widely known at that time. Finally, at age 40, Green entered Cambridge University as an undergraduate but died four years after graduation. In 1846 William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) located a copy of Green’s essay, realized its significan e, and had it reprinted. Green was the first person to try to formulate a mathematical theory of electricity and magnetism. His work was the basis for the subsequent electromagnetic theories of Thomson, Stokes, Rayleigh, and Maxwell.

section.heading: Extended Versions of Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: Although we have proved Green’s Theorem only for the case where $$D$$ is simple, we can now extend it to the case where $$D$$ is a finite union of simple regions. For example, if $$D$$ is the region shown in Figure 6, then we can write $$D = D_{1} \cup D_{2}$$ , where $$D_{1}$$ and $$D_{2}$$ are both simple. The boundary of $$D_{1}$$ is $$C_{1} \cup C_{3}$$ and the boundary of $$D_{2}$$ is $$C_{2} \cup \left( {- C_{3}} \right)$$ so, applying Green’s Theorem to $$D_{1}$$ and $$D_{2}$$ separately, we get

$$\begin{array}{r} {{\int_{C_{1} \cup C_{3}}{Pdx}} + {Qdy} = {\iint\limits_{D_{1}}\left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)dA}} \\ {{\int_{C_{2} \cup ( - C_{3})}{Pdx}} + {Qdy} = {\iint\limits_{D_{2}}\left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right)dA}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A closed curve, two points, and a line segment are displayed. The closed curve resembles a bent rectangle. Imagine a horizontal rectangle with rounded corners bent upward and concave up. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise. A point is marked at the lowest point of the top and bottom sides of the closed curve and the lower one is directly below the upper one. The part of the curve to the left of the points is labeled C_2 and the part of the curve to the right is labeled C_2. A vertical line segment is drawn connecting the two points. A vertical arrow drawn to the left of the line segment points upward and is labeled C_3. Another vertical arrow drawn to the right of the line segment points downward and is labeled negative C_3. The area within the closed curve to the left of the line segment is labeled D_1 and the area to the right of the line segment is labeled D_2.

section.paragraph: If we add these two equations, the line integrals along $$C_{3}$$ and $$- C_{3}$$ cancel, so we get
$$\int_{C_{1} \cup C_{2}}{Pdx + Qdy = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}}$$
which is Green’s Theorem for $$D = D_{1} \cup D_{2}$$ , since its boundary is $$C = C_{1} \cup C_{2}$$ .
The same sort of argument allows us to establish Green’s Theorem for any finite union of nonoverlapping simple regions (see Figure 7).

image.alt: Details A closed loop, three line segments, and six arrows are displayed. The closed loop, labeled C, resembles a curved rectangle. Imagine a long horizontal rectangle bent like an arc. The left end of the rectangle turns and is pulled leftward. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise. Three line segments are drawn within the curve connecting the top and bottom parts of the curve. The first one is vertical and drawn at the highest point of the arc. The second line segment is horizontal and connects the two parts just before the left arm turns. The third line segment is vertical and is drawn near the left end of the closed curve. Each line segment has two arrows drawn near it. The first and third have an arrow pointing upward on the left and a downward pointing arrow on the right. The second horizontal line segment has a leftward pointing arrow above it and a rightward arrow below it.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\oint_{C}{y^{2}dx + 3xydy}$$ , where $$C$$ is the boundary of the semiannular region $$D$$ in the upper half-plane between the circles $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ and $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ .
Solution Notice that although $$D$$ is not simple, the $$y$$ -axis divides it into two simple regions (see Figure 8). In polar coordinates we can write
$$D = \left\{ \left( {r,\theta} \right) \middle| 1 \leqslant r \leqslant 2,0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi \right\}$$
Therefore Green’s Theorem gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\oint_{C}y^{2}dx + 3xydy} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(3xy) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^{2})} \right\rbrack^{}dA}} \\ {\phantom{\oint\limits_{C}y^{2}dx + 3xydy} = {\iint\limits_{D}ydA = \int_{0}^{\pi}\int_{1}^{2}(r\sin\theta)rdrd\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\oint\limits_{C}y^{2}dx + 3xydy} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin\theta d\theta\int_{1}^{2}r^{2}dr = \left\lbrack - \cos\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}r^{3}} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2} = \frac{14}{3}}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details A semiannular region is graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The region remains above the x axis, resting on it with its center at the origin. The boundary of the region resembles two concentric semicircles above the x axis, resting on it, with line segments connecting their starting points and endpoints. The inner semicircle is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 1. An arrowhead placed on the inner semicircle points clockwise. A line segment begins from the end of the inner semicircle on the positive x axis, runs horizontally rightward along the positive x axis, and ends at the end of the outer semicircle on the positive x axis. An arrowhead placed on this line segment points rightward. The outer semicircle is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 4. An arrowhead placed on this semicircle points counterclockwise. From the end of the outer semicircle on the negative x axis, a horizontal line segment runs rightward to meet the end of the inner semicircle on the negative x axis. An arrowhead placed on this line segment points rightward.

section.paragraph: Green’s Theorem can be extended to apply to regions with holes, that is, regions that are not simply-connected. Observe that the boundary $$C$$ of the region $$D$$ in Figure 9 consists of two simple closed curves $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ . We assume that these boundary curves are oriented so that the region $$D$$ is always on the left as the curve $$C$$ is traversed. Thus the positive direction is counterclockwise for the outer curve $$C_{1}$$ but clockwise for the inner curve $$C_{2}$$ . If we divide $$D$$ into two regions $$D^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{''}$$ by means of the lines shown in Figure 10 and then apply Green’s Theorem to each of $$D^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{''}$$ , we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}} = {{\iint\limits_{D^{\prime}}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}} + {\iint\limits_{D^{''}}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA}} = {\int_{\partial D^{\prime}}Pdx + Qdy + \int_{\partial D^{''}}Pdx + Qdy}} \end{array}$$
Since the line integrals along the common boundary lines are in opposite directions, they cancel and we get
$$\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\int_{C_{1}}{Pdx + Qdy + {\int_{C_{2}}{Pdx + Qdy = {\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}}}}}}}$$
which is Green’s Theorem for the region $$D$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right) = \left( {- y\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j}} \right) \slash {({x^{2} + y^{2}})}$$ , show that $$\int_{C}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 2\pi$$ for every positively oriented simple closed path that encloses the origin.

Solution Since $$C$$ is an arbitrary closed path that encloses the origin, it’s difficult to compute the given integral directly. So let’s consider a counterclockwise-oriented circle $$C^{\prime}$$ with center the origin and radius $$a$$ , where $$a$$ is chosen to be small enough that $$C^{\prime}$$ lies inside $$C$$ . (See Figure 11.) Let $$D$$ be the region bounded by $$C$$ and $$C^{\prime}$$ . Then its positively oriented boundary is $$C \cup \left( {- C^{\prime}} \right)$$ and so the general version of Green’s Theorem gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}Pdx + Qdy + \int_{- C^{\prime}}Pdx + Qdy} = {{\iint\limits_{D}\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)}dA}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}Pdx + Qdy + \int_{- C^{\prime}}Pdx + Qdy} = {{\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{{(x^{2} + y^{2})}^{2}} - \frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{{(x^{2} + y^{2})}^{2}}} \right\rbrack}dA = 0}} \end{array}$$
Therefore
$$\int_{C}{Pdx + Qdy = {\int_{C^{\prime}}{Pdx + Qdy}}}$$
that is,
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{C^{\prime}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}}}$$
We now easily compute this last integral using the parametrization given by $$\mathbf{r}(t) = a\cos t\mathbf{i} + a\sin t\mathbf{j}$$ , $$0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\mathbf{F}\left( \mathbf{r}(t) \right) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{F \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}\frac{( - a\sin t)( - a\sin t) + (a\cos t)(a\cos t)}{a^{2}\cos^{2}t + a^{2}\sin^{2}t}}dt = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{dt = 2\pi}}}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details Two simple closed curves and a shaded region are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The first curve, labeled C, almost resembles a rectangle with curved sides and rounded edges, with its right side, bent upward. The curve includes areas from all four quadrants. An arrowhead placed on C points anticlockwise. The second curve, labeled C prime, is a small circle with its center at the origin. An arrowhead placed on C prime points anticlockwise. The region between the two curves is shaded and labeled D.

section.paragraph: We end this section by using Green’s Theorem to discuss a result that was stated in the preceding section.

note.title: Sketch of Proof of Theorem 16.3.6
note.heading: Sketch of Proof of Theorem 16.3.6
note.paragraph: We’re assuming that $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}$$ is a vector field on an open simply-connected region $$D$$ , that $$P$$ and $$Q$$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives, and that
$${\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}} {{throughout}D}$$
If $$C$$ is any simple closed path in $$D$$ and $$R$$ is the region that $$C$$ encloses, then Green’s Theorem gives

$$\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy = {\iint\limits_{R}{\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)dA = {\iint\limits_{R}{0dA = 0}}}}}}}$$

A curve that is not simple crosses itself at one or more points and can be broken up into a number of simple curves. We have shown that the line integrals of $$\mathbf{F}$$ around these simple curves are all $$0$$ and, adding these integrals, we see that $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0}$$ for any closed curve $$C$$ . Therefore $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ is independent of path in $$D$$ by Theorem 16.3.3. It follows that $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a conservative vector field.

section.heading: 16.5. Curl and Divergence
section.paragraph: In this section we define two operations that can be performed on vector fields and that play a basic role in the applications of vector calculus to fluid flow and electricity and magnetism. Each operation resembles differentiation, but one produces a vector field whereas the other produces a scalar field.
section.heading: Curl
section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$ is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ and the partial derivatives of $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ all exist, then the curl of $$\mathbf{F}$$ is the vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ defined by

$${curl}\mathbf{F} = \left( {\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}} \right)\mathbf{i} + \left( {\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x}} \right)\mathbf{j} + \left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)\mathbf{k}$$
As an aid to our memory, let’s rewrite Equation 1 using operator notation. We introduce the vector differential operator $$\nabla$$ (“del”) as
$$\nabla = \mathbf{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x} + \mathbf{j}\frac{\partial}{\partial y} + \mathbf{k}\frac{\partial}{\partial z}$$
It has meaning when it operates on a scalar function to produce the gradient of $$f$$ :

$$\nabla f = \mathbf{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \mathbf{j}\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} + \mathbf{k}\frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\mathbf{k}$$

If we think of $$\nabla$$ as a vector with components $$\partial/\partial x$$ , $$\partial/\partial y$$ , and $$\partial/\partial z$$ , we can also consider the formal cross product of $$\nabla$$ with the vector field $$\mathbf{F}$$ as follows:
So the easiest way to remember Definition 1 is by means of the symbolic expression
$${curl}\mathbf{F} = \nabla \times \mathbf{F}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xz\mathbf{i} + xyz\mathbf{j} - y^{2}\mathbf{k}$$ , find $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ .
Solution Using Equation 2, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = {\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ {xz} & {xyz} & {- y^{2}} \end{matrix} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = {\left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}( - y^{2}) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(xyz)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{i} - \left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}( - y^{2}) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(xz)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{j}}} \\ {\phantom{{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = \left\lbrack \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \right.} + \left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(xyz) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(xz)} \right\rbrack\mathbf{k}} \\ {\phantom{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = {( - 2y - xy)\mathbf{i} - (0 - x)\mathbf{j} + (yz - 0)\mathbf{k}}} \\ {\phantom{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = {- y(2 + x)\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j} + yz\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$

Most computer algebra systems have commands that compute the curl and divergence of vector fields. If you have access to a CAS, use these commands to check the answers to the examples and exercises in this section.

section.paragraph: Recall that the gradient of a function $$f$$ of three variables is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ and so we can compute its curl. The following theorem says that the curl of a gradient vector field is $$0$$ .

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a function of three variables that has continuous second-order partial derivatives, then
$${curl}\left( {\nabla f} \right) = 0$$

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: We have

$$ egin{array}{l} {{{curl}(

by Clairaut’s Theorem.
Notice the similarity to what we know from Section 12.4: $$\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{a} = 0$$ for every three-dimensional vector $$\mathbf{a}$$ .
Since a conservative vector field is one for which $$\mathbf{F} = \nabla f$$ , Theorem 3 can be rephrased as follows:
$${If}\mathbf{F} \text{is conservative, then curl} \mathbf{F} = 0.$$
This gives us a way of verifying that a vector field is not conservative.
Compare this with Exercise 16.3.35.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Show that the vector field $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xz\mathbf{i} + xyz\mathbf{j} - y^{2}\mathbf{k}$$ is not conservative.
Solution In Example 1 we showed that
$${curl}\mathbf{F} = - y\left( {2 + x} \right)\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j} + yz\mathbf{k}$$
This shows that $${curl}\mathbf{F} \neq 0$$ and so, by the remarks preceding this example, $$\mathbf{F}$$ is not conservative.

section.paragraph: The converse of Theorem 3 is not true in general, but the following theorem says the converse is true if $$\mathbf{F}$$ is defined everywhere. (More generally it is true if the domain is simply-connected, that is, “has no hole.”) Theorem 4 is the three-dimensional version of Theorem 16.3.6. Its proof requires Stokes’ Theorem and is sketched at the end of Section 16.8.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a vector field defined on all of $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ whose component functions have continuous partial derivatives and $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ , then $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a conservative vector field.

example.heading: Example 3

list.item: (a) Show that $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = y^{2}z^{3}\mathbf{i} + 2xyz^{3}\mathbf{j} + 3xy^{2}z^{2}\mathbf{k}$$ is a conservative vector field.
(b) Find a function $$f$$ such that $$\mathbf{F} = \nabla f$$ .

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) We compute the curl of $$\mathbf{F}$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = {\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ {y^{2}z^{3}} & {2xyz^{3}} & {3xy^{2}z^{2}} \end{matrix} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = {{(6xyz^{2} - 6xyz^{2})}^{}\mathbf{i} - {(3y^{2}z^{2} - 3y^{2}z^{2})}^{}\mathbf{j} + (2yz^{3} - 2yz^{3})\mathbf{k}}} \\ {\phantom{{curl}\mathbf{F}} = 0} \end{array}$$ Since $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ and the domain of $$\mathbf{F}$$ is $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a conservative vector field by Theorem 4.

(b) The technique for finding $$f$$ was given in Section 16.3. We have $$f_{x}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = y^{2}z^{3}$$ $$f_{y}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 2xyz^{3}$$ $$f_{z}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 3xy^{2}z^{2}$$ Integrating (5) with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xy^{2}z^{3} + g\left( {y,z} \right)$$

example.paragraph: Differentiating (8) with respect to $$y$$ , we get $$f_{y}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 2xyz^{3} + g_{y}\left( {y,z} \right)$$ , so comparison with (6) gives $$g_{y}\left( {y,z} \right) = 0$$ . Thus $$g\left( {y,z} \right) = h(z)$$ and
$$f_{z}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 3xy^{2}z^{2} + h^{\prime}(z)$$
Then (7) gives $$h^{\prime}(z) = 0$$ . Therefore
$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xy^{2}z^{3} + K$$

section.paragraph: The reason for the name curl is that the curl vector is associated with rotations. One connection is explained in Exercise 39. Another occurs when $$\mathbf{F}$$ represents the velocity field in fluid flow (see Example 16.1.3). In Section 16.8 we show that particles near $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in the fluid tend to rotate about the axis that points in the direction of $${curl}\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ , following the right-hand rule, and the length of this curl vector is a measure of how quickly the particles move around the axis (see Figure 1). If $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ at a point $$P$$ , then the fluid is free from rotations at $$P$$ and $$\mathbf{F}$$ is called irrotational at $$P$$ . In this case, a tiny paddle wheel moves with the fluid but doesn’t rotate about its axis. If $${curl}\mathbf{F} \neq 0$$ , the paddle wheel rotates about its axis.

section.paragraph: In Section 16.8 we give a more detailed explanation of curl and its interpretation (as a consequence of Stokes' Theorem).
section.heading: Divergence
section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$ is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ and $$\partial P/\partial x$$ , $$\partial Q/\partial y$$ and $$\partial R/\partial z$$ exist, then the divergence of $$\mathbf{F}$$ is the function of three variables defined by
$${div}\mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}$$

(If $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ , then $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ is a function of two variables defined similarly to the three-variable case.) Observe that $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ is a vector field but $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ is a scalar field. In terms of the gradient operator $$
abla = \left( {\partial/\partial x} ight)\mathbf{i} + \left( {\partial/\partial y} ight)\mathbf{j} + \left( {\partial/\partial z} ight)\mathbf{k}$$ , the divergence of $$\mathbf{F}$$ can be written symbolically as the dot product of $$
abla$$ and $$\mathbf{F}$$ : , the divergence of $$\mathbf{F}$$ can be written symbolically as the dot product of $$
abla$$ and $$\mathbf{F}$$ :
$${div}\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xz\mathbf{i} + xyz\mathbf{j} - y^{2}\mathbf{k}$$ , find $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ .
Solution By the definition of divergence (Equation 9 or 10), we have
$${div}\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {xz} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {xyz} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}{({- y^{2}})} = z + xz$$

section.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , then $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ is also a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . As such, we can compute its divergence. The next theorem shows that the result is $$0$$ .

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$ is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ and $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ have continuous second-order partial derivatives, then
$${div}{curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: Using the definitions of divergence and curl, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{div}{curl}\mathbf{F} = \nabla \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{F})} \\ {\phantom{{div}{curl}\mathbf{F}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x}} \right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{{div}{curl}\mathbf{F}} = \frac{\partial^{2}R}{\partial x\partial y} - \frac{\partial^{2}Q}{\partial x\partial z} + \frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial y\partial z} - \frac{\partial^{2}R}{\partial y\partial x} + \frac{\partial^{2}Q}{\partial z\partial x} - \frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z\partial y}} \\ {\phantom{{div}{curl}\mathbf{F}} = 0} \end{array}$$
because the terms cancel in pairs by Clairaut’s Theorem.
Note the analogy with the scalar triple product: $$\mathbf{a} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}} \right) = 0$$ .

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Show that the vector field $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xz\mathbf{i} + xyz\mathbf{j} - y^{2}\mathbf{k}$$ can’t be written as the curl of another vector field, that is, $$\mathbf{F} \neq {curl}\mathbf{G}$$ for any vector field $$\mathbf{G}$$ .
Solution In Example 4 we showed that
$${div}\mathbf{F} = z + xz$$
and therefore $${div}\mathbf{F} \neq 0$$ . If it were true that $$\mathbf{F} = {curl}\mathbf{G}$$ , then Theorem 11 would give
$${div}\mathbf{F} = {div}{curl}\mathbf{G} = 0$$
which contradicts $${div}\mathbf{F} \neq 0$$ . Therefore $$\mathbf{F}$$ is not the curl of another vector field.

section.paragraph: Again, the reason for the name divergence can be understood in the context of fluid flow. If $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is the velocity of a fluid (or gas), then $${div}\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ represents the net rate of change (with respect to time) of the mass of fluid (or gas) flowing from the point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ per unit volume. In other words, $${div}\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ measures the tendency of the fluid to diverge from the point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ . If $${div}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ , then $$\mathbf{F}$$ is said to be incompressible.
The reason for this interpretation of $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ will be explained at the end of Section 16.9 as a consequence of the Divergence Theorem.

As an illustration, each vector field $$\mathbf{F}$$ in Figure 3 represents the velocity field of a fluid. In Figure 3(a), $${div}\mathbf{F} \neq 0$$ in general. For instance, at the point $$P_{1}$$ , $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ is negative (the vectors that start near $$P_{1}$$ are shorter than those that end near $$P_{1}$$ , so the net flow is inward there). At the point $$P_{2}$$ , $${div}\mathbf{F}$$ is positive (the vectors that start near $$P_{2}$$ are longer than those that end near $$P_{2}$$ , so the net flow is outward there). In Figure 3(b), $${div}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ everywhere (the vectors that start and end near any point $$P$$ are about the same length).

$$
abla^{2} =

$$\nabla^{2}f = \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial x^{2}} + \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial y^{2}} + \frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial z^{2}} = 0$$
We can also apply the Laplace operator $$\nabla^{2}$$ to a vector field

section.heading: Vector Forms of Green’s Theorem
section.paragraph: The curl and divergence operators allow us to rewrite Green’s Theorem in versions that will be useful in our later work. We suppose that the plane region $$D$$ , its boundary curve $$C$$ , and the functions $$P$$ and $$Q$$ satisfy the hypotheses of Green’s Theorem. Then we consider the vector field $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j}$$ . Its line integral is
$$\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\oint_{C}{Pdx + Qdy}}}$$
and, regarding $$\mathbf{F}$$ as a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ with third component $$0$$ , we have

$${curl}\mathbf{F} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ {P(x,y)} & {Q(x,y)} & 0 \end{matrix} \right| = \left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)\mathbf{k}$$
Therefore

$$\left( {{curl}\mathbf{F}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{k} = \left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right){\mathbf{k}} \cdot \mathbf{k} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}$$
and we can now rewrite the equation in Green’s Theorem in the vector form
$${\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T}ds}} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {curl}\mathbf{F} \right) \cdot \mathbf{k}dA}}$$

Equation 12 expresses the line integral of the tangential component of $$\mathbf{F}$$ along $$C$$ as the double integral of the vertical component of $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ over the region $$D$$ enclosed by $$C$$ . We now derive a similar formula involving the normal component of $$\mathbf{F}$$ .
If $$C$$ is given by the vector equation
$$\mathbf{r}(t) = x(t)\mathbf{i} + y(t)\mathbf{j} {a \leqslant t \leqslant b}$$
then the unit tangent vector (see Section 13.2) is
$$\mathbf{T}(t) = \frac{x^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|}\mathbf{i} + \frac{y^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|}\mathbf{j}$$
You can verify that the outward unit normal vector to $$C$$ is given by
$$\mathbf{n}(t) = \frac{y^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|}\mathbf{i} - \frac{x^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|}\mathbf{j}$$
(See Figure 4.) Then, from Equation 16.2.3, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left( {\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}} \right)(t)\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}ds}}{= {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {\frac{P{({x(t),y(t)})}y^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|} - \frac{Q{({x(t),y(t)})}x^{\prime}(t)}{\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|}} \right\rbrack\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}ds}}{= {\int_{a}^{b}{P{({x(t),y(t)})}y^{\prime}(t)dt - Q\left( {x(t),y(t)} \right)x^{\prime}(t)dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}ds}}{= {\int_{C}{Pdy - Qdx = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}} \right)dA}}}}}} \end{array}$$
by Green’s Theorem. But the integrand in this double integral is just the divergence of $$\mathbf{F}$$ . So we have a second vector form of Green’s Theorem.

The closed curve, labeled C, resembles a rectangle with curved sides and rounded corners, curved concave up. The region within the curve is shaded and labeled D. section.paragraph: $$\oint_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}ds = {\iint\limits_{D}{{div}\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}$$

This version says that the line integral of the normal component of $$\mathbf{F}$$ along $$C$$ is equal to the double integral of the divergence of $$\mathbf{F}$$ over the region $$D$$ enclosed by $$C$$ .

Recall from Section 14.3 that a function $$g$$ is called harmonic on $$D$$ if it satisfies Laplace’s equation, that is, $$\nabla^{2}g = 0$$ on $$D$$ . Use Green’s first identity (with the same hypotheses as in Exercise 35) to show that if $$g$$ is harmonic on $$D$$ , then $$\oint_{C}{D_{\mathbf{n}}gds = 0}$$ . Here $$D_{\mathbf{n}}g$$ is the normal derivative of $$g$$ defined in Exercise 35.

Use Green’s first identity to show that if $$f$$ is harmonic on $$D$$ , and if $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ on the boundary curve $$C$$ , then $$\iint_{D}{\left| {\nabla f} \right|^{2}dA = 0}$$ . (Assume the same hypotheses as in Exercise 35.)

This exercise demonstrates a connection between the curl vector and rotations. Let $$B$$ be a rigid body rotating about the $$z$$ -axis. The rotation can be described by the vector $$\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{\omega}\mathbf{k}$$ , where $$\omega$$ is the angular speed of $$B$$ , that is, the tangential speed of any point $$P$$ in $$B$$ divided by the distance $$d$$ from the axis of rotation. Let $$\mathbf{r} = {\langle{x,y,z}\rangle}$$ be the position vector of $$P$$ .

list.item: By considering the angle $$\theta$$ in the figure, show that the velocity field of $$B$$ is given by $$\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{r}$$ .
Show that $$\mathbf{v} = - \omega y\mathbf{i} + \omega x\mathbf{j}$$ .

Show that $${curl}\mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{w}$$ . Details A three-dimensional rendering of a circular disk, 11 vectors, a line segment, and a curved arrow is graphed in the x y z coordinate plane. A curved arrow around this vector points counterclockwise. problem.paragraph: Maxwell’s equations relating the electric field $$\mathbf{E}$$ and magnetic field $$\mathbf{H}$$ as they vary with time in a region containing no charge and no current can be stated as follows:

$$\begin{array}{llllll} {{div}\mathbf{E}} & = & 0 & { {{div}\mathbf{H}}} & = & 0 \\ {{curl}\mathbf{E}} & = & {- \frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial\mathbf{H}}{\partial t}} & { {{curl}\mathbf{H}}} & = & {\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}} \end{array}$$
where $$c$$ is the speed of light. Use these equations to prove the following:

list.item: $$\nabla \times \left( {\nabla \times \mathbf{E}} \right) = - \frac{1}{c^{ 2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^{2}}$$
$$\nabla \times \left( {\nabla \times \mathbf{H}} \right) = - \frac{1}{c^{ 2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{H}}{\partial t^{2}}$$
$$\nabla^{2}\mathbf{E} = \frac{1}{c^{ 2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{E}}{\partial t^{2}}$$ [Hint: Use Exercise 31.]
$$\nabla^{2}\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{c^{ 2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathbf{H}}{\partial t^{2}}$$

problem.paragraph: We have seen that all vector fields of the form $$\mathbf{F} = \nabla g$$ satisfy the equation $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ and that all vector fields of the form $$\mathbf{F} = {curl}\mathbf{G}$$ satisfy the equation $${div}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ (assuming continuity of the appropriate partial derivatives). This suggests the question: are there any equations that all functions of the form $$f = {div}\mathbf{G}$$ must satisfy? Show that the answer to this question is “no” by proving that every continuous function $$f$$ on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ is the divergence of some vector field.
[Hint: Let $$\mathbf{G}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = {\langle{g\left( {x,y,z} \right),0,0}\rangle}$$ , where $$g\left( {x,y,z} \right) = {\int_{0}^{x}{f\left( {t,y,z} \right)dt}}$$ .]

section.heading: 16.6. Parametric Surfaces and Their Areas
section.paragraph: So far we have considered special types of surfaces: cylinders, quadric surfaces, graphs of functions of two variables, and level surfaces of functions of three variables. Here we use vector functions to describe more general surfaces, called parametric surfaces, and compute their areas. Then we take the general surface area formula and see how it applies to special surfaces.
section.heading: Parametric Surfaces
section.paragraph: In much the same way that we describe a space curve by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}(t)$$ of a single parameter $$t$$ , we can describe a surface by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ of two parameters $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ . We suppose that
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{i} + y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{j} + z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{k}$$

is a vector-valued function defined on a region $$D$$ in the $$u\upsilon$$ -plane. So $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , the component functions of $$\mathbf{r}$$ , are functions of the two variables $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ with domain $$D$$ . The set of all points $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ such that
$${x = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)} {y = y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)} {z = z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)}$$

and $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ varies throughout $$D$$ , is called a parametric surface $$S$$ and Equations 2 are called parametric equations of $$S$$ . Each choice of $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ gives a point on $$S$$ ; by making all choices, we get all of $$S$$ . In other words, the surface $$S$$ is traced out by the tip of the position vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ as $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ moves throughout the region $$D$$ . (See Figure 1.)

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, an irregular simple closed curve is drawn in u v plane. Most of the curve lies in the first quadrant, a small portion lies in the fourth quadrant, and a tiny portion in the second quadrant. The region within is shaded and labeled D. A point is marked near and above the positive x axis, within D, and is labeled (u, v). A horizontal arrow, labeled r, points rightward to the second part. In the second part, a curved surface, a point, and a vector are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x-axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface labeled S rises like a dome from a kidney-shaped closed curve. A point is marked within the surface. A vector labeled vector r(u, v) begins at the origin, slopes upward to the right, and reaches the point.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Identify and sketch the surface with vector equation
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = 2\cos u\mathbf{i} + \upsilon\mathbf{j} + 2\sin u\mathbf{k}$$
Solution The parametric equations for this surface are
$${x = 2\cos u} {y = \upsilon} {z = 2\sin u}$$
So for any point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ on the surface, we have

This means that vertical cross-sections parallel to the $$xz$$ -plane (that is, with $$y$$ constant) are all circles with radius $$2$$ . Since $$y = \upsilon$$ and no restriction is placed on $$\upsilon$$ , the surface is a circular cylinder with radius $$2$$ whose axis is the $$y$$ -axis (see Figure 2).

image.alt: Details A three-dimensional rendering of a cylinder and a circle are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The cylinder has its center at the origin and the y axis as its axis. A vertical trace drawn on the surface of the cylinder is a circle with its center at the origin and crosses the positive x and z axes at ((2, 0, 0) and (0, 0, 2), respectively.

section.paragraph: In Example 1 we placed no restrictions on the parameters $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ and so we obtained the entire cylinder. If, for instance, we restrict $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ by writing the parameter domain as
$${0 \leqslant u \leqslant \pi \slash 2} {0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 3}$$
then $$x \geqslant 0$$ , $$z \geqslant 0$$ , $$0 \leqslant y \leqslant 3$$ , and we get the quarter-cylinder with length $$3$$ illustrated in Figure 3.

image.alt: Details A curved surface and a point are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface resembles a curved rectangle with its horizontal base and top side on the XY plane and the y z plane, respectively. The left and right sides resemble quarter circles and are on the x z plane and parallel to the x z plane, respectively. A point is marked on the top right corner of the surface and labeled (0, 3, 2).

section.paragraph: If a parametric surface $$S$$ is given by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ , then there are two useful families of curves that lie on $$S$$ , one family with $$u$$ constant and the other with $$\upsilon$$ constant. These families correspond to vertical and horizontal lines in the $$u\upsilon$$ -plane. If we keep $$u$$ constant by putting $$u = u_{0}$$ , then $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon} \right)$$ becomes a vector function of the single parameter $$\upsilon$$ and defines a curve $$C_{1}$$ lying on $$S$$ . (See Figure 4.)

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, an irregular simple closed curve is drawn in u v plane. Most of the curve lies in the first quadrant, a small portion lies in the fourth octant, and a tiny portion in the second quadrant. The region within is shaded and labeled D. A horizontal line, labeled v = v_0, runs parallel to the x-axis, within the closed curve. A vertical line, labeled u = u_0, runs parallel to the y axis, within the closed curve, crossing the horizontal line at a point labeled (u_0, v_0). A horizontal arrow, labeled r, points rightward to the second part. In the second part, a curved surface and two curves are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface resembles a curved rectangle with its longer sides parallel to the y z plane. Imagine a rectangle at a certain height above the x y plane, parallel to it, with rounded edges and left and right sides bulging outward. The right side is bent 90 degrees downward. The surface rises like a dome above the curved rectangle. Two vertical traces are drawn on the surface. The first one, labeled C_1, is a curve parallel to the x z plane and is a concave down curve running along the middle of the surface, parallel to its shorter sides. The second curve, labeled C_2, is a curve parallel to the y z plane and is a concave down curve running along the middle of the surface, parallel to its longer sides.

section.paragraph: Visual 16.6 shows animated versions of Figures 4 and 5, with moving grid curves, for several parametric surfaces.

Similarly, if we keep $$\upsilon$$ constant by putting $$\upsilon = \upsilon_{0}$$ , we get a curve $$C_{2}$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ that lies on $$S$$ . We call these curves grid curves. (In Example 1, for instance, the grid curves obtained by letting $$u$$ be constant are horizontal lines, whereas the grid curves with $$\upsilon$$ constant are circles.) In fact, when a computer graphs a parametric surface, it sometimes depicts the surface by plotting these grid curves, as we will see in the following example.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Use a computer to graph the surface
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = {\langle{\left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\cos u,\left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\sin u,u + \cos\upsilon}\rangle}$$
Which grid curves have $$u$$ constant? Which have $$\upsilon$$ constant?

Solution We graph the portion of the surface with parameter domain $$0 \leqslant u \leqslant 4\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant \upsilon \leqslant 2\pi$$ in Figure 5. It has the appearance of a spiral tube. To identify the grid curves, we write the corresponding parametric equations:
$${x = \left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\cos u} {y = \left( {2 + \sin\upsilon} \right)\sin u} {z = u + \cos\upsilon}$$

If $$\upsilon$$ is constant, then $$\sin\upsilon$$ and $$\cos\upsilon$$ are constant, so the parametric equations resemble those of the helix in Example 13.1.4. Thus the grid curves with $$\upsilon$$ constant are the spiral curves in Figure 5. We deduce that the grid curves with $$u$$ constant must be the curves that look like circles in the figure. Further evidence for this assertion is that if $$u$$ is kept constant, $$u = u_{0}$$ , then the equation $$z = u_{0} + \cos\upsilon$$ shows that the $$z$$ -values vary from $$u_{0} - 1$$ to $$u_{0} + 1$$ .

image.alt: Details A curved surface is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface resembles a tube coiled around the z-axis like a spring. The surface begins from the x z plane with its center on the x axis, coils around the positive z axis twice as it rises, and ends with its top end on the x z plane. Curves are drawn on the curved surface. Spiral curves parallel to its long run along the length of the surface and are labeled v constant. The curves drawn perpendicular to its length are circles and ellipses placed at equal intervals along the length of the surface and are labeled u constant.

section.paragraph: In Examples 1 and 2 we were given a vector equation and asked to graph the corresponding parametric surface. In the following examples, however, we are given the more challenging problem of finding a vector function to represent a given surface. In the rest of this chapter we will often need to do exactly that.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find a vector function that represents the plane that passes through the point $$P_{0}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}_{0}$$ and that contains two nonparallel vectors $$\mathbf{a}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ .

Solution If $$P$$ is any point in the plane, we can get from $$P_{0}$$ to $$P$$ by moving a certain distance in the direction of $$\mathbf{a}$$ and another distance in the direction of $$\mathbf{b}$$ . So there are scalars $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ such that $$\overset{\rightarrow}{P_{0}P} = u\mathbf{a} + v\mathbf{b}$$ . (Figure 6 illustrates how this works, by means of the Parallelogram Law, for the case where $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are positive. See also Exercise 12.2.46.) If $$\mathbf{r}$$ is the position vector of $$P$$ , then
$$\mathbf{r} = \overset{\rightarrow}{OP_{0}} + \overset{\rightarrow}{P_{0}P} = \mathbf{r}_{0} + u\mathbf{a} + \upsilon\mathbf{b}$$
So the vector equation of the plane can be written as
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = \mathbf{r}_{0} + u\mathbf{a} + \upsilon\mathbf{b}$$
where $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ are real numbers.

image.alt: Details A plane and five vectors are displayed. The plane is shaped like a parallelogram tilted slightly down and to the right. The bottom left corner of the parallelogram is labeled P_0 and its top right corner is labeled P. A vector begins at P_0 and ends at P. The second vector runs along the entire length of the bottom side and is labeled u vector a. The third vector also runs along the bottom side but is shorter than the second and is labeled vector a. The fourth vector runs along the entire length of the left side and is labeled v vector b. The fifth vector also runs along the left side but is shorter than the fourth and is labeled vector b.

example.paragraph: If we write $$\mathbf{r} = {\langle{x,y,z}\rangle}$$ , $$\mathbf{r}_{0} = {\langle{x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}}\rangle}$$ , $$\mathbf{a} = {\langle{a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}}\rangle}$$ , and $$\mathbf{b} = {\langle{b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}}\rangle}$$ , then we can write the parametric equations of the plane through the point $$\left( {x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ as follows:

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find a parametric representation of the sphere

Solution The sphere has a simple representation $$\rho = a$$ in spherical coordinates, so let’s choose the angles $$\phi$$ and $$\theta$$ in spherical coordinates as the parameters (see Section 15.8). Then, putting $$\rho = a$$ in the equations for conversion from spherical to rectangular coordinates (Equations 15.8.1), we obtain
$$x = {a\sin\phi\cos\theta} y = {a\sin\phi\sin\theta} z = {a\cos\phi}$$
as the parametric equations of the sphere. The corresponding vector equation is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = a\sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + a\sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + a\cos\phi\mathbf{k}$$

We have $$0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi$$ and $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , so the parameter domain is the rectangle $$D = \left\lbrack {0,\pi} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,2\pi} \right\rbrack$$ . The grid curves with $$\phi$$ constant are the circles of constant latitude (including the equator). The grid curves with $$\theta$$ constant are the meridians (semicircles), which connect the north and south poles (see Figure 7).

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, a vertical rectangle is graphed in the first quadrant of the phi theta plane. There are two tick marks on the phi axis: c and pi, with c to the left of pi. There are two tick marks on the theta axis: k and 2 pi, with k below 2 pi. The rectangle has its left side along the positive theta axis with its top left corner at the tick mark 2 pi and its base along the positive phi axis with its bottom right corner at the tick mark pi. The region within the rectangle is shaded and labeled D. From the tick mark c on the phi axis, a vertical line, labeled phi = c, runs parallel to the positive theta axis to meet the top side of the rectangle. From the tick mark k on the theta axis, a horizontal line labeled theta = k, runs parallel to the positive phi axis, crosses the vertical line and meets the right side of the rectangle. A horizontal arrow points rightward to the second part. In the second part, a sphere is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The sphere has its center at the origin. Two horizontal traces are drawn on the sphere. One falls on the x y plane and is a circle with its center at the origin. The second horizontal trace, labeled phi = c, lies above and is parallel to the first. It is a smaller circle with its center on the positive z axis. A vertical trace, labeled theta = k, passes through the z axis and the x y plane.

section.paragraph: Note We saw in Example 4 that the grid curves for a sphere are curves of constant latitude or constant longitude. For a general parametric surface we are really making a map and the grid curves are similar to lines of latitude and longitude. Describing a point on a parametric surface (like the one in Figure 5) by giving specific values of $$u$$ and $$\upsilon$$ is like giving the latitude and longitude of a point.

One of the uses of parametric surfaces is in computer graphics. Figure 8 shows the result of trying to graph the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ by solving the equation for $$z$$ and graphing the top and bottom hemispheres separately. Part of the sphere appears to be missing because of the rectangular grid system used by the software. The much better picture in Figure 9 was produced by a computer using the parametric equations found in Example 4.

image.alt: Details The figure displays many gridded curves. The curved surfaces resemble curved rectangles. Perpendicular rectangles are bent concave down with their tips pointing downward. All the rectangles together appear to be lying on the top half of a sphere. The bottom half of the arrangement is a reflection of the top half with the tips of the corresponding rectangles pointing toward each other.
Details A sphere is displayed. Horizontal and vertical traces drawn on the sphere resemble latitudes and longitudes on a globe.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find a parametric representation for the cylinder
$${x^{2} + y^{2} = 4} {0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1}$$

Solution The cylinder has a simple representation $$r = 2$$ in cylindrical coordinates, so we choose as parameters $$\theta$$ and $$z$$ in cylindrical coordinates. Then the parametric equations of the cylinder are
$$x = {2\cos\theta} y = {2\sin\theta} z = z$$
where $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ and $$0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1$$ . In vector notation,
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\theta,z} \right) = 2\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + 2\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + z\mathbf{k}$$
and the vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ maps the parameter domain
$$D = \left\{ (\theta,z) \middle| 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi,0 \leq z \leq 1 \right\}$$
to a cylinder, as shown in Figure 10

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, a horizontal rectangle is graphed in the first quadrant of the theta z plane. There are two tick marks on the theta axis: c and 2 pi, with c to the left of 2 pi. There are two tick marks on the z-axis: k and 1, with k below 1. The rectangle has its left side along the positive z-axis with its top left corner at the tick mark 1 and its base along the positive theta axis with its bottom right corner at the tick mark 2 pi. The region within the rectangle is shaded and labeled D. From the tick mark c on the theta axis, a vertical line runs parallel to the positive z axis to meet the top side of the rectangle. From the tick mark k on the z axis, a horizontal line runs parallel to the positive theta axis, crosses the vertical line, and meets the right side of the rectangle. A horizontal arrow points rightward to the second part. In the second part, a cylinder is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The cylinder has a circular base on the x y plane with the center of the base at the origin and a circular top surface with its center at (0, 0, 1). A horizontal trace labeled z = k, drawn on the surface of the cylinder is a circle parallel to the x y plane with its center on the positive z axis. A vertical line, labeled theta = c, begins from the circumference of the base on the first quadrant of the x y plane and rises vertically upward, parallel to the positive z axis.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find a vector function that represents the elliptic paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + 2y^{2}$$ .
Solution If we regard $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters, then the parametric equations are simply
and the vector equation is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {x,y} \right) = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + {({x^{2} + 2y^{2}})}^{}\mathbf{k}$$

section.paragraph: In general, a surface given as the graph of a function of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , that is, with an equation of the form $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , can always be regarded as a parametric surface by taking $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters and writing the parametric equations as
$$x = x y = y z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$
In Module 16.6 you can investigate several families of parametric surfaces.
Parametric representations (also called parametrizations) of surfaces are not unique. The next example shows two ways to parametrize a cone.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find a parametric representation for the surface $$z = 2\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ , that is, the top half of the cone $$z^{2} = 4x^{2} + 4y^{2}$$ .
Solution 1 One possible representation is obtained by choosing $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters:
So the vector equation is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {x,y} \right) = x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\mathbf{k}$$

Solution 2 Another representation results from choosing as parameters the polar coordinates $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ . A point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ on the cone satisfies $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$y = r\sin\theta$$ , and $$z = 2\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} = 2r$$ . So a vector equation for the cone is
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {r,\theta} \right) = r\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + r\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + 2r\mathbf{k}$$
where $$r \geqslant 0$$ and $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ .

For some purposes the parametric representations in Solutions 1 and 2 of Example 7 are equally good, but Solution 2 might be preferable in certain situations. If we are interested only in the part of the cone that lies below the plane $$z = 1$$ , for instance, all we have to do in Solution 2 is change the parameter domain to
$$D = \left\{ (r,\theta)|0 \leq r \leq \frac{1}{2},0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}$$
Then the vector function $$\mathbf{r}$$ maps the region $$D$$ to the half-cone shown in Figure 11.

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, a horizontal rectangle is graphed in the first quadrant of the theta r plane. There are two tick marks on the theta axis: c and 2 pi, with c to the left of 2 pi. There are two tick marks on the r axis: k and 1/2, with k below 1/2. The rectangle has its left side along the positive r axis with its top left corner at the tick mark 1/2 and its base along the positive theta axis with its bottom right corner at the tick mark 2 pi. The region within the rectangle is shaded and labeled D. From the tick mark c on the theta axis, a vertical line runs parallel to the positive r axis to meet the top side of the rectangle. From the tick mark k on the r axis, a horizontal line runs parallel to the positive theta axis, crosses the vertical line, and meets the right side of the rectangle. A horizontal arrow points rightward to the second part. In the second part, an inverted cone is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The cone has its tip at the origin, the positive z-axis as its axis, and opens upward until a height of 1 along the positive z axis. A horizontal trace, labeled r = k, drawn on the surface of the cone is a circle parallel to the x y plane with its center on the positive z-axis. A line, labeled theta = c, begins from the origin and slopes upward along the slanted side of the cone in the first octant.

section.heading: Surfaces of Revolution
section.paragraph: Surfaces of revolution can be represented parametrically. For instance, let’s consider the surface $$S$$ obtained by rotating the curve $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , about the $$x$$ -axis, where $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ . Let $$\theta$$ be the angle of rotation as shown in Figure 12. If $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is a point on $$S$$ , then
$$x = x y = f(x)\cos\theta z = f(x)\sin\theta$$

Therefore we take $$x$$ and $$\theta$$ as parameters and regard Equations 3 as parametric equations of $$S$$ . The parameter domain is given by $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ .

image.alt: Details A three-dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid resembles a horizontal long cylinder with its axis along the positive x axis and its back circular surface smaller than its front circular one. The centers of the back and front circular faces are on the positive x axis. A curve is drawn on the x y plane, along the curved side of the solid and is labeled y = f(x). Two horizontal line segments begin from the center of the front face of the solid, and end at its circumference, both are labeled f(x). One of them is horizontal and lies on the x y plane. The second one slopes upward to the right, at an angle theta from the horizontal line segment, to meet the circumference at a point labeled (x, y, z). From this point, a dashed vertical line segment, labeled z, descends downward to meet the horizontal line segment at right angles to it.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Find parametric equations for the surface generated by rotating the curve $$y = \sin x$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ , about the $$x$$ -axis. Use these equations to graph the surface of revolution.
Solution From Equations 3, the parametric equations are
$${x = x} {y = \sin x\cos\theta} {z = \sin x\sin\theta}$$
and the parameter domain is $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 2\pi$$ , $$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$ . Using a computer to plot these equations, we obtain the graph in Figure 13.

image.alt: Details A gridded closed surface is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x-axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive y axis slopes up and slightly to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The surface begins at the origin, bulges away from the positive x axis in all directions, and then approaches and meets the axis, and repeats this pattern once again. The two parts of the gridded surface resemble an ellipsoid with pointed narrow sides.

section.paragraph: We can adapt Equations 3 to represent a surface obtained through revolution about the $$y$$ - or $$z$$ -axis (see Exercise 30).
section.heading: Tangent Planes
section.paragraph: We now find the tangent plane to a parametric surface $$S$$ traced out by a vector function
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{i} + y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{j} + z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{k}$$

at a point $$P_{0}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ . If we keep $$u$$ constant by putting $$u = u_{0}$$ , then $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon} \right)$$ becomes a vector function of the single parameter $$\upsilon$$ and defines a grid curve $$C_{1}$$ lying on $$S$$ . (See Figure 14.) The tangent vector to $$C_{1}$$ at $$P_{0}$$ is obtained by taking the partial derivative of $$\mathbf{r}$$ with respect to $$\upsilon$$ :

$$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial\upsilon}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{k}$$

Similarly, if we keep $$\upsilon$$ constant by putting $$\upsilon = \upsilon_{0}$$ , we get a grid curve $$C_{2}$$ given by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon_{0}} \right)$$ that lies on $$S$$ , and its tangent vector at $$P_{0}$$ is

$$\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\left( {u_{0},\upsilon_{0}} \right)_{}\mathbf{k}$$

If $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ is not $$0$$ , then the surface $$S$$ is called smooth (it has no “corners”). For a smooth surface, the tangent plane is the plane that contains the tangent vectors $$\mathbf{r}_{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ , and the vector $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}$$ is a normal vector to the tangent plane.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Find the tangent plane to the surface with parametric equations $$x = u^{2}$$ , $$y = \upsilon^{2}$$ , $$z = u + 2\upsilon$$ at the point $$\left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ .
Solution We first compute the tangent vectors:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\mathbf{k} = 2u\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{k}} \\ {\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial\upsilon}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial\upsilon}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial\upsilon}\mathbf{k} = 2\upsilon\mathbf{j} + 2\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$
Thus a normal vector to the tangent plane is

$$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {2u} & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & {2v} & 2 \end{matrix} \right| = - 2v\mathbf{i} - 4u\mathbf{j} + 4\mathit{uv}\mathbf{k}$$
Notice that the point $$\left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ corresponds to the parameter values $$u = 1$$ and $$\upsilon = 1$$ , so the normal vector there is
$$- 2\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}$$
Therefore an equation of the tangent plane at $$\left( {1,1,3} \right)$$ is
$$- 2\left( {x - 1} \right) - 4\left( {y - 1} \right) + 4\left( {z - 3} \right) = 0$$
or
