section.heading: Surface Area
section.paragraph: Now we define the surface area of a general parametric surface given by Equation 1. For simplicity we start by considering a surface $$S$$ whose parameter domain $$D$$ is a rectangle, and we divide it into subrectangles $$R_{ij}$$ . Let’s choose $$({u_{i}^{*},\upsilon_{j}^{*}})$$ to be the lower left corner of $$R_{ij}$$ . (See Figure 16.)

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, a rectangular grid and a shaded region are the first quadrants of u v plane. The region within the rectangle is labeled D. One of the squares in the grid is shaded and labeled R_(i j). The bottom side of the square is labeled Delta u and the right side is labeled Delta v. A horizontal arrow, labeled r, points rightward from the first part to the second part. In the second part, the rectangular grid from the first part is transformed into a curved surface with grid lines. The curved rectangular surface has its shorter sides parallel to the x z plane and the x y plane and the longer sides parallel to the y z plane and x y plane. The rectangle is tilted to the right and bulges outward to the front and slightly to the right. The same rectangle which was shaded in the first part is shaded in the second part as well and labeled S_(i j). A point marked near the bottom left corner of the square is labeled P(i j).

figure.caption: The image of the subrectangle $$R_{ij}$$ is the patch $$S_{ij}$$ .

section.paragraph: The part $$S_{ij}$$ of the surface $$S$$ that corresponds to $$R_{ij}$$ is called a patch and has the point $$P_{ij}$$ with position vector $$\mathbf{r}{({u_{i}^{*},v_{j}^{*}})}$$ as one of its corners. Let
and
$$\mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}^{*} = \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}{({u_{i}^{*},v_{j}^{*}})}$$
be the tangent vectors at $$P_{ij}$$ as given by Equations 5 and 4.

Figure 17(a) shows how the two edges of the patch that meet at $$P_{ij}$$ can be approximated by vectors. These vectors, in turn, can be approximated by the vectors $$\Delta u\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*}$$ and $$\Delta\upsilon\mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}$$ because partial derivatives can be approximated by difference quotients. So we approximate $$S_{ij}$$ by the parallelogram determined by the vectors $$\Delta u\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*}$$ and $$\Delta\upsilon\mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}$$ . This parallelogram is shown in Figure 17(b) and lies in the tangent plane to $$S$$ at $$P_{ij}$$ . The area of this parallelogram is

$$\left| {\left( {\Delta u\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*}} \right) \times \left( {\Delta\upsilon\mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}} \right)} \right| = \left| {\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}} \right|\Delta u\Delta\upsilon$$
and so an approximation to the area of $$S$$ is
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u}^{*} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}^{*}} \right|\Delta u\Delta\upsilon}}$$

Our intuition tells us that this approximation gets better as we increase the number of subrectangles, and we recognize the double sum as a Riemann sum for the double integral $$\iint_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}} \right|dud\upsilon}$$ . This motivates the following definition.

The second vector begins from P_(i j), slopes slightly upward to the right, and meets the top left corner of the rectangle. The other rectangle is of a similar size with straight sides, lies above the curved one, and is tangent to it at both their bottom left corners. A vector labeled Delta u vector r^*_u runs along the bottom side of the tangent rectangle. The second vector labeled Delta-v vector r^*_v runs along the left side of the tangent rectangle.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: If a smooth parametric surface $$S$$ is given by the equation

$${\mathbf{r}\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) = x\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{i} + y\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{j} + z\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)\mathbf{k}} {\left( {u,\upsilon} \right) \in D}$$
and $$S$$ is covered just once as $$\left( {u,\upsilon} \right)$$ ranges throughout the parameter domain $$D$$ , then the surface area of $$S$$ is
$$A(S) = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{\upsilon}} \right|dA}}$$
where

$${\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\mathbf{k}} {\mathbf{r}_{v} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\mathbf{k}}$$

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius $$a$$ .
Solution In Example 4 we found the parametric representation
$${x = a\sin\phi\cos\theta} {y = a\sin\phi\sin\theta} {z = a\cos\phi}$$
where the parameter domain is
$$D = \left\{ (\phi,\theta) \middle| 0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi,0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi \right\}$$
We first compute the cross product of the tangent vectors:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial\phi} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\phi} & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\phi} \\ \frac{\partial x}{\partial\theta} & \frac{\partial y}{\partial\theta} & \frac{\partial z}{\partial\theta} \end{matrix} \right| = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {a\cos\phi\cos\theta} & {a\cos\phi\sin\theta} & {- a\sin\phi} \\ {- a\sin\phi\sin\theta} & {a\sin\phi\cos\theta} & 0 \end{matrix} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}}{= a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + a^{2}\sin\phi\cos\phi\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$
Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right| = \sqrt{a^{4}{\sin}^{4}\phi{\cos}^{2}\theta + a^{4}{\sin}^{4}\phi{\sin}^{2}\theta + a^{4}{\sin}^{2}\phi{\cos}^{2}\phi^{}}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {r_{\phi} \times r_{\theta}} \right|}{= \sqrt{a^{4}{\sin}^{4}\phi + a^{4}{\sin}^{2}\phi{\cos}^{2}\phi^{}} = a^{2}\sqrt{{\sin}^{2}\phi^{}} = a^{2}\sin\phi}} \end{array}$$
since $$\sin\phi \geqslant 0$$ for $$0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi$$ . Therefore, by Definition 6, the area of the sphere is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right|dA = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{a^{2}\sin\phi d\phi d\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= a^{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin\phi d\phi = a^{2}\left( {2\pi} \right)2 = 4\pi a^{2}}}}}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Surface Area of the Graph of a Function
section.paragraph: For the special case of a surface $$S$$ with equation $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , where $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ lies in $$D$$ and $$f$$ has continuous partial derivatives, we take $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters. The parametric equations are
$${x = x} {y = y} {z = f\left( {x,y} \right)}$$
so
$${\mathbf{r}_{x} = \mathbf{i} + \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right)\mathbf{k}} {\mathbf{r}_{y} = \mathbf{j} + \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right)\mathbf{k}}$$
and

$$\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \end{matrix} \right| = - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$
Thus we have

$$|\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y}| = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right)^{2} + 1} = \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}$$
and the surface area formula in Definition 6 becomes
$$A(S) = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}dA}}$$
Notice the similarity between the surface area formula in Equation 9 and the arc length formula
$$L = {\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}}dx$$
from Section 8.1.

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Find the area of the part of the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ that lies under the plane $$z = 9$$ .

Solution The plane intersects the paraboloid in the circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 9$$ , $$z = 9$$ . Therefore the given surface lies above the disk $$D$$ with center the origin and radius $$3$$ . (See Figure 18.) Using Formula 9, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + \left( {2x} \right)^{2} + \left( {2y} \right)^{2}}dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= {\iint\limits_{D}{\sqrt{1 + 4{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}}dA}}}} \end{array}$$
Converting to polar coordinates, we obtain

image.alt: Details A three-dimensional rendering of a paraboloid and a shaded region is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y-axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The paraboloid has its vertex at the origin and opens upward until the tick mark 9 on the positive z axis. The shaded region is circular and lies on the x y plane. It is labeled D, has it's center at the origin, and crosses the x axis at x = 3.

section.paragraph: The question remains whether our definition of surface area (6) is consistent with the surface area formula from single-variable calculus (8.2.4).

We consider the surface $$S$$ obtained by rotating the curve $$y = f(x)$$ , $$a \leqslant x \leqslant b$$ , about the $$x$$ -axis, where $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ is continuous. From Equations 3 we know that parametric equations of $$S$$ are
$$x = x y = f(x)\cos\theta z = f(x)\sin\theta a \leqslant x \leqslant b 0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$
To compute the surface area of $$S$$ we need the tangent vectors

$$\begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{r}_{x} & = & {\mathbf{i} + f^{\prime}(x)\cos\theta\mathbf{j} + f^{\prime}(x)\sin\theta\mathbf{k}} \\ \mathbf{r}_{\theta} & = & {- f(x)\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + f(x)\cos\theta\mathbf{k}} \end{array}$$
Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & {f^{\prime}(x)\cos\theta} & {f^{\prime}(x)\sin\theta} \\ 0 & {- f(x)\sin\theta} & {f(x)\cos\theta} \end{matrix} \right|} \\ {\phantom{\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}}{= f(x)f^{\prime}(x)\mathbf{i} - f(x)\cos\theta\mathbf{j} - f(x)\sin\theta\mathbf{k}}} \end{array}$$
and so

$$\begin{array}{l} {|\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}| = \sqrt{{\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{2}{\lbrack f^{\prime}(x)\rbrack}^{2} + {\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta + {\lbrack f(x)\rbrack}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}} \\ {\phantom{\left| r_{x} \times r_{\theta} \right|} = \sqrt{\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}\left\lbrack {1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}} \right\rbrack^{}} = f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}} \end{array}$$
because $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ . Therefore the area of $$S$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right|_{}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}dxd\theta}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= 2\pi{\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)\sqrt{1 + \left\lbrack {f^{\prime}(x)} \right\rbrack^{2}}dx}}}} \end{array}$$
This is precisely the formula that was used to define the area of a surface of revolution in single-variable calculus (8.2.4).

section.heading: 16.7. Surface Integrals
section.paragraph: The relationship between surface integrals and surface area is much the same as the relationship between line integrals and arc length. Suppose $$f$$ is a function of three variables whose domain includes a surface $$S$$ . We will define the surface integral of $$f$$ over $$S$$ in such a way that, in the case where $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 1$$ , the value of the surface integral is equal to the surface area of $$S$$ . We start with parametric surfaces and then deal with the special case where $$S$$ is the graph of a function of two variables.
section.heading: Parametric Surfaces
section.paragraph: Suppose that a surface $$S$$ has a vector equation
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,v} \right) = x\left( {u,v} \right)\mathbf{i} + y\left( {u,v} \right)\mathbf{j} + z\left( {u,v} \right)\mathbf{k}\left( {u,v} \right) \in D$$

We first assume that the parameter domain $$D$$ is a rectangle and we divide it into subrect angles $$R_{ij}$$ with dimensions $$\Delta u$$ and $$\Delta v$$ . Then the surface $$S$$ is divided into corresponding patches $$S_{ij}$$ as in Figure 1.

image.alt: Details The figure has two connected parts. In the first part, a rectangular grid and a shaded region are the first quadrants of u v plane. The region within the rectangle is labeled D. One of the squares in the grid is shaded and labeled R_(i j). The bottom side of the square is labeled Delta u and the right side is labeled Delta v. A horizontal arrow, labeled r, points rightward from the first part to the second part. In the second part, the rectangular grid from the first part is transformed into a curved surface with grid lines. The curved rectangular surface has its shorter sides parallel to the x z plane and the x y plane and the longer sides parallel to the y z plane and x y plane. The left portion of the rectangle is almost horizontal and lies above the x y plane. The rectangle then goes down to the right, initially concave down and then concave up and meets the x y plane and very briefly lies on the x y plane. The same rectangle which was shaded in the first part is shaded in the second part as well and labeled S_(i j). A point marked near the top left corner of the square is labeled P^*(i j.

section.paragraph: We evaluate $$f$$ at a point $$P_{ij}^{*}$$ in each patch, multiply by the area $$\Delta S_{ij}$$ of the patch, and form the Riemann sum
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{f{(P_{ij}^{*})}\Delta S_{ij}}}$$
Then we take the limit as the number of patches increases and define the surface integral of $$\mathbf{f}$$ over the surface $$\mathbf{S}$$ as
$$\iint\limits_{S}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS = \lim\limits_{m,n\rightarrow\infty}{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{m}{\sum\limits_{j = 1}^{n}{f{(P_{ij}^{*})}\Delta S_{ij}}}}}$$
Notice the analogy with the definition of a line integral (16.2.2) and also the analogy with the definition of a double integral (15.1.5).

To evaluate the surface integral in Equation 1 we approximate the patch area $$\Delta S_{ij}$$ by the area of an approximating parallelogram in the tangent plane. In our discussion of surface area in Section 16.6 we made the approximation
$$\Delta S_{ij} \approx \left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|\Delta u \Delta v$$
where

$$\mathbf{r}_{u} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\mathbf{k}\mathbf{r}_{v} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\mathbf{i} + \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}\mathbf{j} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\mathbf{k}$$

are the tangent vectors at a corner of $$S_{ij}$$ . If the components are continuous and $$\mathbf{r}_{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{r}_{v}$$ are nonzero and nonparallel in the interior of $$D$$ , it can be shown from Definition 1, even when $$D$$ is not a rectangle, that
$$\iint\limits_{S}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)dS = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {\mathbf{r}\left( {u,v} \right)} \right)\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|dA}}}$$
We assume that the surface is covered only once as $$\left( {u,v} \right)$$ ranges throughout $$D$$ . The value of the surface integral does not depend on the parametrization that is used.
This should be compared with the formula for a line integral:
$$\int_{C}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)ds = {\int_{a}^{b}{f\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right)\left| {\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)} \right|dt}}}$$
Observe also that
$$\iint\limits_{S}{1dS = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|dA = A(S)}}}$$

Formula 2 allows us to compute a surface integral by converting it into a double integral over the parameter domain $$D$$ . When using this formula, remember that $$f{({\mathbf{r}\left( {u,v} \right)})}$$ is evaluated by writing $$x = x\left( {u,v} \right)$$ , $$y = y\left( {u,v} \right)$$ , and $$z = z\left( {u,v} \right)$$ in the formula for $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ .

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Compute the surface integral $$\iint_{S}{x^{2}dS}$$ , where $$S$$ is the unit sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ .
Solution As in Example 16.6.4, we use the parametric representation
$$x = \sin\phi\cos\theta y = \sin\phi\sin\theta z = \cos\phi 0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi 0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$
that is,
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = \sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + \sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + \cos\phi\mathbf{k}$$
As in Example 16.6.10, we can compute that
$$\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right| = \sin\phi$$
Therefore, by Formula 2,

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{S}x^{2}dS} = {\iint\limits_{D}{(\sin\phi\cos\theta)}^{2}\left| \mathbf{r}_{\phi} \right. \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}\left| dA \right.}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}x^{2}dS} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}\phi\cos^{2}\theta\sin\phi d\phi d\theta = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\cos^{2}\theta d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{3}\phi d\phi}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}x^{2}dS} = {{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)d\theta}}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{(\sin\phi - \sin\phi\cos^{2}\phi)d\phi}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}x^{2}dS} = {\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack {- \cos\phi + \frac{1}{3}\cos^{3}\phi} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = \frac{4\pi}{3}}} \end{array}$$
Here we use the identities
$$\begin{array}{lll} {\cos^{2}\theta} & = & {\frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)} \\ {\sin^{2}\phi} & = & {1 - \cos^{2}\phi} \end{array}$$
Instead, we could use Formulas 64 and 67 in the Table of Integrals.

section.paragraph: Surface integrals have applications similar to those for the integrals we have previously considered. For example, if a thin sheet (say, of aluminum foil) has the shape of a surface $$S$$ and the density (mass per unit area) at the point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ , then the total mass of the sheet is
$$m = {\iint\limits_{S}{\rho{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS}}$$
and the center of mass is $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y},\overline{z}} \right)$$ , where

$$\overline{x} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{S}{x\rho{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS}} \overline{y} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{S}{y\rho{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS}} \overline{z} = \frac{1}{m}{\iint\limits_{S}{z\rho{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS}}$$
Moments of inertia can also be defined as before (see Exercise 41).
section.heading: Graphs of Functions
section.paragraph: Any surface $$S$$ with equation $$z = g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ can be regarded as a parametric surface with parametric equations
$$x = x y = y z = g\left( {x,y} \right)$$
and so we have
$$\mathbf{r}_{x} = \mathbf{i} + \left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \right)\mathbf{k} \mathbf{r}_{y} = \mathbf{j} + \left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} \right)\mathbf{k}$$
Thus
$$\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y} = - \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$$
and
$$\left| {\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y}} \right| = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2} + 1}$$
Therefore, in this case, Formula 2 becomes

$$\iint\limits_{S}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,y,g\left( {x,y} \right)} \right)\sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2} + 1}dA}}}$$

Similar formulas apply when it is more convenient to project $$S$$ onto the $$yz$$ -plane or $$xz$$ -plane. For instance, if $$S$$ is a surface with equation $$y = h\left( {x,z} \right)$$ and $$D$$ is its projection onto the $$xz$$ -plane, then

$$\iint\limits_{S}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)dS = {\iint\limits_{D}{f\left( {x,h\left( {x,z} \right),z} \right)\sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial y}{\partial z} \right)^{2} + 1}dA}}}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint_{S}{ydS}$$ , where $$S$$ is the surface $$z = x + y^{2}$$ , $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$$ , $$0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2$$ . (See Figure 2.)

image.alt: Details A curved surface is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the right. The positive y axis slopes slightly up and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface is a grid curve that resembles a curved rectangular sheet with its back left corner at the origin, and the front left corner elevated from the positive x axis. The rectangular sheet rises upward to the right, concave up.

example.paragraph: Solution Since
$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = 1$$
and
$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = 2y$$
Formula 4 gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{ydS = {\iint\limits_{D}{y\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{ydS}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{2}{y\sqrt{1 + 1 + 4y^{2}}dydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{ydS}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{dx\sqrt{2}{\int_{0}^{2}{y\sqrt{1 + 2y^{2}}dy}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{ydS}} = {\sqrt{2}\left( \frac{1}{4} \right)\frac{2}{3}{({1 + 2y^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2}\rbrack_{0}^{2}} = \frac{13\sqrt{2}}{3}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: If $$S$$ is a piecewise-smooth surface, that is, a finite union of smooth surfaces $$S_{1},S_{2},\ldots,S_{n}$$ that intersect only along their boundaries, then the surface integral of $$f$$ over $$S$$ is defined by
$$\iint\limits_{S}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS = {\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS + \cdots + {\iint\limits_{S_{n}}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}dS}}}}}$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint_{S}{zdS}$$ , where $$S$$ is the surface whose sides $$S_{1}$$ are given by the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , whose bottom $$S_{2}$$ is the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1$$ in the plane $$z = 0$$ , and whose top $$S_{3}$$ is the part of the plane $$z = 1 + x$$ that lies above $$S_{2}$$ .

Solution The surface $$S$$ is shown in Figure 3. (We have changed the usual position of the axes to get a better look at $$S$$ .) For $$S_{1}$$ we use $$\theta$$ and $$z$$ as parameters (see Example 16.6.5) and write its parametric equations as
$$x = \cos\theta y = \sin\theta z = z$$
where
$$0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$
and
$$0 \leqslant z \leqslant 1 + x = 1 + \cos\theta$$
Therefore

$$\mathbf{r}_{\theta} \times \mathbf{r}_{z} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ {- \sin\theta} & {\cos\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{matrix} \right| = \cos\theta\mathbf{i} + \sin\theta\mathbf{j}$$
and
$$\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\theta} \times \mathbf{r}_{z}} \right| = \sqrt{\cos^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\theta} = 1$$

image.alt: Details A three-dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes slightly up and to the right. The positive y axis slopes up and to the left. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid has three surfaces and resembles a cylinder cut diagonally into half. It has a circular base, a curved side, and a top surface resembling an ellipse. The base of the cylinder, labeled S_2, is a circle with its center at the origin. The curved surface of the cylinder, labeled S_1(x^2 + y^2 = 1) resembles a triangle with its bottom corners brought together on the negative x axis and the bottom side resting on the base circle. The third side, labeled S_3(z = 1 + x), resembles an ellipse tilted down and to the left, with its center on the positive z axis. The highest point of the ellipse is one of its narrow sides and lies directly above the positive x-axis and the lowest point is the other narrow side and lies on the negative x axis.

example.paragraph: Thus the surface integral over $$S_{1}$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{zdS = {\iint\limits_{D}{z\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\theta} \times \mathbf{r}_{z}} \right|dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{zdS}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1 + \cos\theta}{zdzd\theta = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos\theta} \right)^{2}d\theta}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{zdS}} = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\lbrack {1 + 2\cos\theta + \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos 2\theta} \right)} \right\rbrack d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{zdS}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{3}{2}\theta + 2\sin\theta + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi} = \frac{3\pi}{2}} \end{array}$$
Since $$S_{2}$$ lies in the plane $$z = 0$$ , we have
$$\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{zdS = {\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{0dS = 0}}}$$

The top surface $$S_{3}$$ lies above the unit disk $$D$$ and is part of the plane $$z = 1 + x$$ . So, taking $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 1 + x$$ in Formula 4 and converting to polar coordinates, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S_{3}}{zdS = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {1 + x} \right)\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{3}}{zdS}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {1 + r\cos\theta} \right)\sqrt{1 + 1 + 0}rdrd\theta}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{3}}{zdS}} = \sqrt{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({r + r^{2}\cos\theta})}drd\theta}}} = \sqrt{2}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\left( {\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3}\cos\theta} \right)}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{3}}{zdS}} = \sqrt{2}\left\lbrack {\frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin\theta}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi} = \sqrt{2}\pi} \end{array}$$
Therefore

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{zdS = {\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{zdS + {\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{zdS + {\iint\limits_{S_{3}}{zdS}}}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{zdS}} = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 0 + \sqrt{2}\pi = \left( {\frac{3}{2} + \sqrt{2}} \right)\pi} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Oriented Surfaces
section.paragraph: To define surface integrals of vector fields, we need to rule out nonorientable surfaces such as the Möbius strip shown in Figure 4. [It is named after the German geometer August Möbius (1790–1868).] You can construct one for yourself by taking a long rectangular strip of paper, giving it a half-twist, and taping the short edges together as in Figure 5. If an ant were to crawl along the Möbius strip starting at a point $$P$$ , it would end up on the “other side” of the strip (that is, with its upper side pointing in the opposite direction). Then, if the ant continued to crawl in the same direction, it would end up back at the same point $$P$$ without ever having crossed an edge. (If you have constructed a Möbius strip, try drawing a pencil line down the middle.) Therefore a Möbius strip really has only one side. You can graph the Möbius strip using the parametric equations in Exercise 16.6.32.

image.alt: Details The figure displayed a Mobius strip and many vectors. Imagine a thin rectangular strip whose edges have been fused after a twist has been added. A point labeled P is marked directly opposite to twice. Many vectors are drawn perpendicular to the strip at equal intervals. The vectors on the left of the twist and the point inward and the vectors on the right of the point and the twice point outward.

Details The figure has two parts. The first part is a thin horizontal rectangular strip with its bottom left, top left, top right, and bottom right corners labeled A, B, C, and D, respectively. In the second part, the rectangular strip is twisted once and its ends are brought toward each other such that A and C and B and D face each other.

section.paragraph: From now on we consider only orientable (two-sided) surfaces. We start with a surface $$S$$ that has a tangent plane at every point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ on $$S$$ (except at any boundary point). There are two unit normal vectors $$\mathbf{n}_{1}$$ and $$\mathbf{n}_{2} = - \mathbf{n}_{1}$$ at $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ . (See Figure 6.)

image.alt: Details A curved surface and two vectors are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface resembles a square, parallel to the x y plane, curved concave down. The sides of the squares are concave down curves. The front right corner of the square has been pulled down to meet the x y plane. A point is marked at the center of the curved surface. A vector, labeled vector n_1, slopes upward to the right, perpendicular to the surface, from the point. Another vector, labeled vector n_2, slopes down to the left, perpendicular to the surface, from the point and is the exact opposite of vector n_1.

section.paragraph: If it is possible to choose a unit normal vector $$\mathbf{n}$$ at every such point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ so that $$\mathbf{n}$$ varies continuously over $$S$$ , then $$S$$ is called an oriented surface and the given choice of $$\mathbf{n}$$ provides $$S$$ with an orientation. For any orientable surface, there are two possible orientations (see Figure 7).

image.alt: Details The figure has two parts, both parts contain the same curved surface and four vectors. The curved surface resembles a square, parallel to the x y plane, curved concave down. The sides of the squares are concave down curves. The front right corner of the square has been pulled down lower than the other three. Four points are marked such that they lie at equal intervals midway between the front and back edges of the curved surface. From each of the points, a vector rises perpendicular to the surface. All four of them are labeled vector n. The first vector is almost vertical but slopes slightly to the left, the second vector is almost vertical but slopes slightly to the right, the third vector slopes upward to the right, and the fourth vector is almost horizontal but slopes slightly upward to the right. The vectors seem to point radially outward from the surface. In the second part, the four vectors begin from the same points and are perpendicular to the surface, but are placed below the surface, pointing toward the center of curvature of the surface. All the vectors are labeled vector n.

figure.caption: The two orientations of an orientable surface

section.paragraph: For a surface $$z = g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ given as the graph of $$g$$ , we use Equation 3 to associate with the surface a natural orientation given by the unit normal vector

$$\mathbf{n} = \frac{- \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} \right)^{2}}}$$
Since the $$\mathbf{k}$$ -component is positive, this gives the upward orientation of the surface.

If $$S$$ is a smooth orientable surface given in parametric form by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,v} \right)$$ , then it is automatically supplied with the orientation of the unit normal vector
$$\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|}$$
and the opposite orientation is given by $$- \mathbf{n}$$ . For instance, in Example 16.6.4 we found the parametric representation
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = a\sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + a\sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + a\cos\phi\mathbf{k}$$
for the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = a^{2}$$ . Then in Example 16.6.10 we found that
$$\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta} = a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + a^{2}\sin^{2}\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + a^{2}\sin\phi\cos\phi\mathbf{k}$$
and
$$\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right| = a^{2}\sin\phi$$
So the orientation induced by $$\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right)$$ is defined by the unit normal vector

$$\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right|} = \sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + \sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + \cos\phi\mathbf{k} = \frac{1}{a}\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right)$$

Observe that $$\mathbf{n}$$ points in the same direction as the position vector, that is, outward from the sphere (see Figure 8). The opposite (inward) orientation would have been obtained (see Figure 9) if we had reversed the order of the parameters because $$\mathbf{r}_{\theta} \times \mathbf{r}_{\phi} = - \mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}$$ .

The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The sphere has its center at the origin. A horizontal trace drawn on the surface of the sphere lies on the x y plane. It is a circle with its center at the origin. Six points are marked on the surface of the sphere. From each of the six points, a vector is drawn on the surface of the sphere, perpendicular to it. They point radially away from the center.

Details A sphere and six vectors are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x-axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The sphere has its center at the origin. A horizontal trace drawn on the surface of the sphere lies on the x y plane. It is a circle with its center at the origin. Six points are marked on the surface of the sphere. From each of the six points, a vector is drawn within the sphere, perpendicular to the curved surface of the sphere. All the vectors point toward the center of the sphere.

section.paragraph: For a closed surface, that is, a surface that is the boundary of a solid region $$E$$ , the convention is that the positive orientation is the one for which the normal vectors point outward from $$E$$ , and inward-pointing normals give the negative orientation (see Figures 8 and 9).
section.heading: Surface Integrals of Vector Fields; Flux
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$S$$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $$\mathbf{n}$$ , and imagine a fluid with density $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ and velocity field $$\mathbf{v}\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ flowing through $$S$$ . (Think of $$S$$ as an imaginary surface that doesn’t impede the fluid flow, like a fishing net across a stream.) Then the rate of flow (mass per unit time) per unit area is given by the vector field $$\rho\mathbf{v}$$ . (See Figure 10.)

image.alt: Details A vector field and a curved surface are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x-axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface, labeled S, resembles a rectangle with curved sides and rounded edges. The surface is bent slightly concave down. The vector field, labeled vector F = rho vector v, rises from the bottom. The vectors near the x z plane are almost vertical but slope slightly to the right. The vectors progressively slope more as we proceed to the right and become almost horizontal but slightly sloping upward as we reach the right side of the viewing window. Some vectors pass through S and one vector that begins from the surface and is tangent to it is made bold.

section.paragraph: If we divide $$S$$ into small patches $$S_{ij}$$ , as in Figure 11 (compare with Figure 1), then $$S_{ij}$$ is nearly planar and so we can approximate the mass of fluid per unit time crossing $$S_{ij}$$ in the direction of the normal $$\mathbf{n}$$ by the quantity
$$\left( {\rho\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}} \right)A{(S_{ij})}$$

where $$\rho$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\mathbf{n}$$ are evaluated at some point on $$S_{ij}$$ . (Recall that the component of the vector $$\rho\mathbf{v}$$ in the direction of the unit vector $$\mathbf{n}$$ is $$\rho\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}$$ .) By summing these quantities and taking the limit we get, according to Definition 1, the surface integral of the function $$\rho\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}$$ over $$S$$ :
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\rho\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS = {\iint\limits_{S}{\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right){\mathbf{v}}\left( {x,y,z} \right) \cdot \mathbf{n}\left( {x,y,z} \right)dS}}}$$
and this is interpreted physically as the rate of flow through $$S$$ .

image.alt: Details A curved surface, a shaded region, and two vectors are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curved surface, labeled S, resembles a rectangle with curved sides and rounded edges. The surface is bent slightly concave down. A small square path is shaded on the curved surface and is labeled S_(i j). A vector, labeled vector F = rho vector v, begins from the shaded region and is tangent to the surface. Another vector labeled vector n begins from the same point vector F does and slopes upward to the right. It is perpendicular to the surface and vector F.

section.paragraph: If we write $$\mathbf{F} = \rho\mathbf{v}$$ , then $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a vector field on $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ and the integral given in Equation 7 becomes
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS}$$
A surface integral of this form occurs frequently in physics, even when $$\mathbf{F}$$ is not $$\rho\mathbf{v}$$ , and is called the surface integral (or flux integral) of $$\mathbf{F}$$ over $$S$$ .

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{F}$$ is a continuous vector field defined on an oriented surface $$S$$ with unit normal vector $$\mathbf{n}$$ , then the surface integral of $$\mathbf{F}$$ over $$\mathbf{S}$$ is
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS}}}$$
This integral is also called the flux of $$\mathbf{F}$$ across $$S$$ .

section.paragraph: In words, Definition 8 says that the surface integral of a vector field over $$S$$ is equal to the surface integral of its normal component over $$S$$ (as previously defined).
If $$S$$ is given by a vector function $$\mathbf{r}\left( {u,v} \right)$$ , then $$\mathbf{n}$$ is given by Equation 6, and from Definition 8 and Equation 2 we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS}} = {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|}dS}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot dS}}{= \iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}\left( {u,v} \right)} \right) \cdot \frac{\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}}{\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|}} \right\rbrack\left| {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right|dA}} \end{array}$$
where $$D$$ is the parameter domain. Thus we have
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}} \right)dA}}}$$
Formula 9 assumes the orientation of $$S$$ induced by $$\mathbf{r}_{u} \times \mathbf{r}_{v}$$ , as in Equation 6. For the opposite orientation, we multiply by $$- 1$$ .
Compare Equation 9 to the similar expression for evaluating line integrals of vector fields in Definition 16.2.13:
$$\int_{C}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\mathbf{F}{({\mathbf{r}{(t)}})} \cdot}}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}{(t)}dt$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find the flux of the vector field $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = z\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + x\mathbf{k}$$ across the unit sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ .
Solution As in Example 1, we use the parametric representation
$$\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right) = \sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + \sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + \cos\phi\mathbf{k} 0 \leqslant \phi \leqslant \pi 0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi$$
Then
$$\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right)} \right) = \cos\phi\mathbf{i} + \sin\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + \sin\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{k}$$
and, from Example 16.6.10,
$$\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta} = \sin^{2}\phi\cos\theta\mathbf{i} + \sin^{2}\phi\sin\theta\mathbf{j} + \sin\phi\cos\phi\mathbf{k}$$
(You can check that these vectors correspond to the outward orientation of the sphere.) Therefore

$$\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}\left( {\phi,\theta} \right)} \right) \cdot \left( {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right) = \cos\phi\sin^{2}\phi\cos\theta + \sin^{3}\phi\sin^{2}\theta + \sin^{2}\phi\cos\phi\cos\theta$$
and, by Formula 9, the flux is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{r}_{\phi} \times \mathbf{r}_{\theta}} \right)dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{{({2\sin^{2}\phi\cos\phi\cos\theta + \sin^{3}\phi\sin^{2}\theta})}d\phi d\theta}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = 2{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}\phi\cos\phi d\phi{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\cos\theta d\theta + {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{3}\phi d\phi{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\sin^{2}\theta d\theta}}}}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = 0 + \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{3}\phi d\phi\int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin^{2}\theta d\theta \left( {{since}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\cos\theta d\theta = 0}}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = \frac{4\pi}{3}} \end{array}$$
by the same calculation as in Example 1.
Figure 12 shows the vector field $$\mathbf{F}$$ in Example 4 at points on the unit sphere.

image.alt: Details A sphere and a vector field are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The sphere has its center at the origin. Equidistant horizontal and vertical traces on the surface of the sphere resemble latitudes and longitudes. The vectors slope upward and are tangent to the sphere in the front and are tangential and slope downward as we move around the sphere to its back.

section.paragraph: If, for instance, the vector field in Example 4 is a velocity field describing the flow of a fluid with density $$1$$ , then the answer, $$4\pi \slash 3$$ , represents the rate of flow through the unit sphere in units of mass per unit time.
In the case of a surface $$S$$ given by a graph $$z = g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , we can think of $$x$$ and $$y$$ as parameters and use Equation 3 to write

$$\mathbf{F} \cdot \left( {\mathbf{r}_{x} \times \mathbf{r}_{y}} \right) = \left( {P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}} \right) \cdot \left( {- \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\mathbf{i} - \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}} \right)$$
Thus Formula 9 becomes
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {- P\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R} \right)dA}}}$$

This formula assumes the upward orientation of $$S$$ ; for a downward orientation we multiply by $$- 1$$ . Similar formulas can be worked out if $$S$$ is given by $$y = h\left( {x,z} \right)$$ or $$x = k\left( {y,z} \right)$$ . (See Exercises 37 and 38.)

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iint_{S}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}$$ , where $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = y\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j} + z\mathbf{k}$$ and $$S$$ is the boundary of the solid region $$E$$ enclosed by the paraboloid $$z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ and the plane $$z = 0$$ .

Solution $$S$$ consists of a parabolic top surface $$S_{1}$$ and a circular bottom surface $$S_{2}$$ . (See Figure 13.) Since $$S$$ is a closed surface, we use the convention of positive (outward) orientation. This means that $$S_{1}$$ is oriented upward and we can use Equation 10 with $$D$$ being the projection of $$S_{1}$$ onto the $$xy$$ -plane, namely, the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1$$ . Since
$$P\left( {x,y,z} \right) = y Q\left( {x,y,z} \right) = x R\left( {x,y,z} \right) = z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$
on $$S_{1}$$ and
$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} = - 2x \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} = - 2y$$
we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {- P\frac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R} \right)dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\iint\limits_{D}{{\lbrack{- y\left( {- 2x} \right) - x\left( {- 2y} \right) + 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}}\rbrack}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\iint\limits_{D}{{({1 + 4xy - x^{2} - y^{2}})}dA}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({1 + 4r^{2}\cos\theta\sin\theta - r^{2}})}rdrd\theta}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({r - r^{3} + 4r^{3}\cos\theta\sin\theta})}drd\theta}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left( {\frac{1}{4} + \cos\theta\sin\theta} \right)d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\left( {2\pi} \right) + 0 = \frac{\pi}{2}}}} \end{array}$$
The disk $$S_{2}$$ is oriented downward, so its unit normal vector is $$\mathbf{n} = - \mathbf{k}$$ and we have

$${\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \left( {- \mathbf{k}} \right)dS = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {- z} \right)dA = {\iint\limits_{D}{0dA = 0}}}}}}}}\mathbf{}$$

since $$z = 0$$ on $$S_{2}$$ . Finally, we compute, by definition, $$\iint_{S}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}$$ as the sum of the surface integrals of $$\mathbf{F}$$ over the pieces $$S_{1}$$ and $$S_{2}$$ :
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} + {\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{\pi}{2} + 0 = \frac{\pi}{2}}}}}}$$

image.alt: Details A three-dimensional rendering of a solid and eight vectors are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x-axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid resembles the tip of a paraboloid opening downward with its vertex on the positive z axis. The paraboloid surface is labeled S_1. Five vectors arise from the curved surface, perpendicular to it. The base of the solid, labeled S_2, is a circle on the x y plane with its center at the origin. Three vectors descend vertically downward from S_2.

section.paragraph: Although we motivated the surface integral of a vector field using the example of fluid flow, this concept also arises in other physical situations. For instance, if $$\mathbf{E}$$ is an electric field (see Example 16.1.5), then the surface integral
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}$$

is called the electric flux of $$\mathbf{E}$$ through the surface $$S$$ . One of the important laws of electrostatics is Gauss’s Law, which says that the net charge enclosed by a closed surface $$S$$ is
$$Q = \varepsilon_{0}{\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}}$$

where $$\varepsilon_{0}$$ is a constant (called the permittivity of free space) that depends on the units used. (In the SI system, $$\varepsilon_{0} \approx 8.8542 \times 10^{- 12}C^{2} \slash N \cdot m^{2}$$ .) Therefore, if the vector field $$\mathbf{F}$$ in Example 4 represents an electric field, we can conclude that the charge enclosed by $$S$$ is $$Q = \frac{4}{3}\pi\varepsilon_{0}$$ .

Another application of surface integrals occurs in the study of heat flow. Suppose the temperature at a point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in a body is $$u\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ . Then the heat flow is defined as the vector field
$$\mathbf{F} = - K\nabla u$$
where $$K$$ is an experimentally determined constant called the conductivity of the substance. The rate of heat flow across the surface $$S$$ in the body is then given by the surface integral
$$\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = - K{\iint\limits_{S}{\nabla u \cdot d\mathbf{S}}}}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: The temperature $$u$$ in a metal ball is proportional to the square of the distance from the center of the ball. Find the rate of heat flow across a sphere $$S$$ of radius $$a$$ with center at the center of the ball.
Solution Taking the center of the ball to be at the origin, we have
where $$C$$ is the proportionality constant. Then the heat flow is
$$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = - K\nabla u = - KC\left( {2x\mathbf{i} + 2y\mathbf{j} + 2z\mathbf{k}} \right)$$

where $$K$$ is the conductivity of the metal. Instead of using the usual parametrization of the sphere as in Example 4, we observe that the outward unit normal to the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = a^{2}$$ at the point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is
$$\mathbf{n} = \frac{1}{a}\left( {x\mathbf{i} + y\mathbf{j} + z\mathbf{k}} \right)$$
and so
$$\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = - \frac{2KC}{a}{({x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}})}$$
But on $$S$$ we have $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = a^{2}$$ , so $$\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = - 2aKC$$ . Therefore the rate of heat flow across $$S$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS = - 2aKC{\iint\limits_{S}{dS}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int\limits_{S}{\int{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}}} = - 2aKCA(S) = - 2aKC{({4\pi a^{2}})} = - 8KC\pi a^{3}} \end{array}$$

exercises.heading: 16.7. Exercises

problem.paragraph: Let $$S$$ be the surface of the box enclosed by the planes $$x = \pm 1$$ , $$y = \pm 1$$ , $$z = \pm 1$$ . Approximate $$\iint_{S}{\cos\left( {x + 2y + 3z} \right)dS}$$ by using a Riemann sum as in Definition 1, taking the patches $$S_{ij}$$ to be the squares that are the faces of the box $$S$$ and the points $$P_{ij}^{*}$$ to be the centers of the squares.
A surface $$S$$ consists of the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , $$- 1 \leqslant z \leqslant 1$$ , together with its top and bottom disks. Suppose you know that $$f$$ is a continuous function with
$$f\left( {\pm 1,0,0} \right) = 2 f\left( {0, \pm 1,0} \right) = 3 f\left( {0,0, \pm 1} \right) = 4$$
Estimate the value of $$\iint_{S}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)dS}$$ by using a Riemann sum, taking the patches $$S_{ij}$$ to be four quarter-cylinders and the top and bottom disks.

Let $$H$$ be the hemisphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 50$$ , $$z \geqslant 0$$ , and suppose $$f$$ is a continuous function with $$f\left( {3,4,5} \right) = 7$$ , $$f\left( {3, - 4,5} \right) = 8$$ , $$f\left( {- 3,4,5} \right) = 9$$ , and $$f\left( {- 3, - 4,5} \right) = 12$$ . section.heading: 16.8. Stokes’ Theorem
section.paragraph: Stokes’ Theorem can be regarded as a higher-dimensional version of Green’s Theorem. Whereas Green’s Theorem relates a double integral over a plane region $$D$$ to a line integral around its plane boundary curve, Stokes’ Theorem relates a surface integral over a surface $$S$$ to a line integral around the boundary curve of $$S$$ (which is a space curve). Figure 1 shows an oriented surface with unit normal vector $$\mathbf{n}$$ . The orientation of $$S$$ induces the positive orientation of the boundary curve $$\mathbf{C}$$ shown in the figure. This means that if you walk in the positive direction around $$C$$ with your head pointing in the direction of $$\mathbf{n}$$ , then the surface will always be on your left.

image.alt: Details A curve, a curved surface, three vectors, and an image of a man walking are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The curve, labeled C, is a closed one and lies above the x y plane, is kidney shaped, concave down. The curved surface, labeled S, bulges upward from the curve. Three vectors, all three labeled vector n, rise upward from S, perpendicular to it. An image of a man waking is placed on the bottom left part of the curve and he faces rightward. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise.

note.title: Stokes’ Theorem
note.heading: Stokes’ Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $$S$$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface that is bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary curve $$C$$ with positive orientation. Let $$\mathbf{F}$$ be a vector field whose components have continuous partial derivatives on an open region in $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ that contains $$S$$ . Then
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}}}$$

section.paragraph: Since
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{T}ds}}}$$
and
$$\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS}}}$$

Stokes’ Theorem says that the line integral around the boundary curve of $$S$$ of the tangential component of $$\mathbf{F}$$ is equal to the surface integral over $$S$$ of the normal component of the curl of $$\mathbf{F}$$ .
The positively oriented boundary curve of the oriented surface $$S$$ is often written as $$\partial S$$ , so Stokes’ Theorem can be expressed as
$$\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\int_{\partial S}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}}}$$

There is an analogy among Stokes’ Theorem, Green’s Theorem, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. As before, there is an integral involving derivatives on the left side of Equation 1 (recall that $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ is a sort of derivative of $$\mathbf{F}$$ ) and the right side involves the values of $$\mathbf{F}$$ only on the boundary of $$\mathbf{S}$$ .

In fact, in the special case where the surface $$S$$ is flat and lies in the $$xy$$ -plane with upward orientation, the unit normal is $$\mathbf{k}$$ , the surface integral becomes a double integral, and Stokes’ Theorem becomes
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S}{\left( {{curl}\mathbf{F}} \right) \cdot \mathbf{k}dA}}}}}$$
This is precisely the vector form of Green’s Theorem given in Equation 16.5.12. Thus we see that Green’s Theorem is really a special case of Stokes’ Theorem.
Although Stokes’ Theorem is too difficult for us to prove in its full generality, we can give a proof when $$S$$ is a graph and $$\mathbf{F}$$ , $$S$$ , and $$C$$ are well behaved.
section.heading: Proof of a Special Case of Stokes’ Theorem
section.paragraph: We assume that the equation of $$S$$ is $$z = g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ , $$\left( {x,y} \right) \in D$$ , where $$g$$ has continuous second-order partial derivatives and $$D$$ is a simple plane region whose boundary curve $$C_{1}$$ corresponds to $$C$$ . If the orientation of $$S$$ is upward, then the positive orientation of $$C$$ corresponds to the positive orientation of $$C_{1}$$ . (See Figure 2.) We are also given that $$\mathbf{F} = P\mathbf{i} + Q\mathbf{j} + R\mathbf{k}$$ , where the partial derivatives of $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ are continuous.

image.alt: Details Two closed curves, a shaded region, four line segments, and a vector are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first closed curve, labeled C, resembles a curved rectangle. It is at a certain height from the x y plane with its longer sides parallel to the y axis and shorter sides parallel to the x axis. The longer sides resemble parallel waves. The back left and front right corners are rounded. Arrowheads placed on C point counterclockwise. The region within the curve is shaded and labeled S and defined by z = g(x, y). S resembles a wavy curved rectangle. A vector, labeled vector n, rises vertically upward from the highest point of S, perpendicular to it. Four vertical dashed line segments descend downward to meet the x y plane at the four corners of the second closed curve. The second closed curve resembles a rectangle, with its sides very slightly bulging outward, and is labeled C_1. Arrowheads placed on C_1 point counterclockwise. The region within C_1 is shaded and labeled D.

section.paragraph: Since $$S$$ is a graph of a function, we can apply Formula 16.7.10 with $$\mathbf{F}$$ replaced by $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ . The result is

$$\iint\limits_{S}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack {- \left( {\frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}} \right)\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} - \left( \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x} \right)\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} + \left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}} \right)} \right\rbrack dA$$
where the partial derivatives of $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ are evaluated at $$\left( {x,y,g\left( {x,y} \right)} \right)$$ . If
$$x = x(t) y = y(t) a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$
is a parametric representation of $$C_{1}$$ , then a parametric representation of $$C$$ is
$$x = x(t) y = y(t) z = g{({x(t),y(t)})} a \leqslant t \leqslant b$$
This allows us, with the aid of the Chain Rule, to evaluate the line integral as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left( {P\frac{dx}{dt} + Q\frac{dy}{dt} + R\frac{dz}{dt}} \right)dt}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {P\frac{dx}{dt} + Q\frac{dy}{dt} + R\left( {\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt} + \frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}} \right)} \right\rbrack dt}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {\left( {P + R\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}} \right)\frac{dx}{dt} + \left( {Q + R\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}} \right)\frac{dy}{dt}} \right\rbrack dt}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{C_{1}}{{\left( {P + R\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}} \right)}dx + \left( {Q + R\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}} \right)dy}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left\lbrack {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left( {Q + R\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}} \right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left( {P + R\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}} \right)} \right\rbrack dA}}} \end{array}$$

where we have used Green’s Theorem in the last step. Then, using the Chain Rule again and remembering that $$P$$ , $$Q$$ , and $$R$$ are functions of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ and that $$z$$ is itself a function of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , we get

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{C}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{D}\left\lbrack \left( {\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial x}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} + R\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial x\partial y}} \right) \right.}} \\ {\left. - \left( {\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial P}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial y}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\frac{\partial z}{\partial x} + R\frac{\partial^{2}z}{\partial y\partial x}} \right) \right\rbrack dA} \end{array}$$
Four of the terms in this double integral cancel and the remaining six terms can be arranged to coincide with the right side of Equation 2. Therefore
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}}}$$

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ , where $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = - y^{2}\mathbf{i} + x\mathbf{j} + z^{2}\mathbf{k}$$ and $$C$$ is the curve of intersection of the plane $$y + z = 2$$ and the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . (Orient $$C$$ to be counterclockwise when viewed from above.)
Solution The curve $$C$$ (an ellipse) is shown in Figure 3. Although $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ could be evaluated directly, it’s easier to use Stokes’ Theorem. We first compute

$${curl}\mathbf{F} = \left| \begin{matrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial}{\partial z} \\ {- y^{2}} & x & z^{2} \end{matrix} \right| = \left( {1 + 2y} \right)\mathbf{k}$$

Stokes’ Theorem allows us to choose any (oriented, piecewise-smooth) surface with boundary curve $$C$$ . Among the many possible such surfaces, the most convenient choice is the elliptical region $$S$$ in the plane $$y + z = 2$$ that is bounded by $$C$$ . If we orient $$S$$ upward, then $$C$$ has the induced positive orientation. The projection $$D$$ of $$S$$ onto the $$xy$$ -plane is the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 1$$ and so using Equation 16.7.10 with $$z = g\left( {x,y} \right) = 2 - y$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint\limits_{S}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left( {1 + 2y} \right)dA}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {1 + 2r\sin\theta} \right)rdrd\theta}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\left\lbrack {\frac{r^{2}}{2} + 2\frac{r^{3}}{3}\sin\theta} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1}d\theta}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{\left( {\frac{1}{2} + \frac{2}{3}\sin\theta} \right)}d\theta}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}} = \frac{1}{2}\left( {2\pi} \right) + 0 = \pi} \end{array}$$

The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid is a cylinder with a slanted cut at its top. The base of the cylinder is circular and is on the x y plane with its center at the origin. The curved surface of the cylinder has the positive z axis as its axis and is labeled x^2 + y^2 = 1. The top surface of the cylinder, labeled S, is a tilted ellipse that slopes toward the x z plane from left to right. It is labeled y + z = 2 and has its center on the positive z-axis. The curve which serves as the boundary for S is labeled C. Arrowheads are placed on the C point counterclockwise.

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: Stokes’ Theorem allows us to compute a surface integral simply by knowing the values of $$\mathbf{F}$$ on the boundary curve $$C$$ . This means that if we have another oriented surface with the same boundary curve $$C$$ , then we get exactly the same value for the surface integral. In general, if $$S_{1}$$ and $$S_{2}$$ are oriented surfaces with the same oriented boundary curve $$C$$ and both satisfy the hypotheses of Stokes’ Theorem, then
$$\iint\limits_{S_{1}}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{S_{2}}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}}}}}$$
This fact is useful when it is difficult to integrate over one surface but easy to integrate over the other.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Use Stokes’ Theorem to compute the integral $$\iint_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}$$ , where $$\mathbf{F}\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xz\mathbf{i} + yz\mathbf{j} + xy\mathbf{k}$$ and $$S$$ is the part of the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ that lies inside the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ and above the $$xy$$ -plane. (See Figure 4.)

image.alt: Details A hemisphere, a cylinder, a circle, and a shaded region are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The hemisphere, labeled x^2 + y^4 +z^2 = 4, has its center at the origin and its base on the x y plane. A cylinder, labeled x^2 +y^=2 = 1, lies within the hemisphere such that its base is on the base of the hemisphere, on the x y plane with the center of its base at the origin. The circular boundary of the top surface of the cylinder, labeled C, touches the inner surface of the hemisphere. An arrowhead is placed on C point counterclockwise. The part of the hemisphere above C is shaded and labeled S

example.paragraph: Solution 1 To find the boundary curve $$C$$ we solve the equations $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 4$$ and $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ . Subtracting, we get $$z^{2} = 3$$ and so $$z = \sqrt{3}$$ (since $$z > 0$$ ). Thus $$C$$ is the circle given by the equations $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , $$z = \sqrt{3}$$ . A vector equation of $$C$$ is
$$\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos t\mathbf{i} + \sin t\mathbf{j} + \sqrt{3}\mathbf{k} 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 2\pi$$
so
$$\mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t) = - \sin t\mathbf{i} + \cos t\mathbf{j}$$
Also, we have
$$\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right) = \sqrt{3}\cos t\mathbf{i} + \sqrt{3}\sin t\mathbf{j} + \cos t\sin t\mathbf{k}$$
Therefore, by Stokes’ Theorem,

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{\mathbf{F}\left( {\mathbf{r}(t)} \right) \cdot \mathbf{r}^{\prime}(t)dt}}}}}} \\ {{\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}} = {\int_{0}^{2\pi}{{({- \sqrt{3}\cos t\sin t + \sqrt{3}\sin t\cos t})}dt}}} = \sqrt{3}{\int_{0}^{2\pi}{0dt = 0}}} \end{array}$$

Solution 2 Let $$S_{1}$$ be the disk in the plane $$z = \sqrt{3}$$ inside the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , as shown in Figure 5. Since $$S_{1}$$ and $$S$$ have the same boundary curve $$C$$ , it follows by Stokes’ Theorem that
$$\iint\limits_{S}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_{1}}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}$$
Because $$S_{1}$$ is part of a horizontal plane, its upward normal is $$\mathbf{k}$$ . We calculate that $${curl}\mathbf{F} = (x - y)\mathbf{i} + (x - y)\mathbf{j}$$ , so

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iint\limits_{S}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_{1}}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_{1}}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n}d\mathbf{S}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{S}{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}} = \iint\limits_{S_{1}}\lbrack(x - y)\mathbf{i} + (x - y)\mathbf{j}\rbrack \cdot \mathbf{k}d\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_{S_{1}}0\mathit{dS} = 0} \end{array}$$

The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The hemisphere, labeled x^2 + y^4 +z^2 = 4, has its center at the origin and its base on the x y plane. A cylinder, labeled x^2 +y^=2 = 1, lies within the hemisphere such that its base is on the base of the hemisphere, on the x y plane with the center of its base at the origin. The circular boundary of the top surface of the cylinder, labeled C, touches the inner surface of the hemisphere. An arrowhead is placed on C point counterclockwise. The top surface, the region within C, is shaded and labeled S_1.

section.paragraph: We now use Stokes’ Theorem to shed some light on the meaning of the curl vector. Suppose that $$C$$ is an oriented closed curve and $$\mathbf{v}$$ represents the velocity field in fluid flow. Consider the line integral
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\int_{C}{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{T}ds}}}$$

and recall that $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{T}$$ is the component of $$\mathbf{v}$$ in the direction of the unit tangent vector $$\mathbf{T}$$ . This means that the closer the direction of $$\mathbf{v}$$ is to the direction of $$\mathbf{T}$$ , the larger the value of $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{T}$$ . (Recall that if $$\mathbf{v}$$ and $$\mathbf{T}$$ point in generally opposite directions, then $$\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{T}$$ is negative.) Thus $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}$$ is a measure of the tendency of the fluid to move around $$C$$ in the same direction as the orientation of $$C$$ , and is called the circulation of $$\mathbf{v}$$ around $$C$$ . (See Figure 6.)

image.alt: Details A vector field, two closed curves, and four vectors are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The vectors enter and exit from both the left and right sides of the viewing window. There are 10 rows of vectors. The first two and last two rows of vectors enter from the top left corner, trace a wave, reaching a minimum in the second quadrant and a maximum in the first quadrant, and exit at the top right corner. The fifth and sixth rows enter from the right and exit at the left, trace a wave about the x-axis, reaching a smaller minimum and maximum near the origin near the positive and negative x-axis, respectively. The vectors in the remaining rows follow the waves. The pattern also resembles a family of three parallel vertical waves with concentric ellipses between the horizontal waves. The first closed curve, labeled C_1, resembles a rounded rectangle and encloses the elliptical pattern which lies mostly in the third and partly in the second quadrants. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise. A vector labeled vector v slopes upward to the left from a point at the top right of C_1 and lies within the curve. Another vector labeled vector T is tangent to C_1 at the same point and is almost vertical and slightly tilted to the left. The second curve, labeled C_2, is slightly larger and longer than the first with its right side bigger than its left, and lies mostly in the first quadrant surrounding an elliptical pattern with a small portion of the curve in the second quadrant. Arrowheads are placed on the curve point counterclockwise. A vector labeled vector v slopes downward to the left from a point at the bottom right of C_2 and lies within the curve. Another vector labeled vector T is tangent to C_2 at the same point and is almost vertical and slightly tilted to the left.

figure.caption: $$\int_{C_{1}}\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r} > 0$$ , positive circulation $$\int_{C_{2}}\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r} < 0$$ , negative circulation

section.paragraph: Now let $$P_{0}\left( {x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}} \right)$$ be a point in the fluid and let $$S_{a}$$ be a small disk with radius $$a$$ and center $$P_{0}$$ . Then $$\left( {{curl}\mathbf{F}} \right)(P) \approx \left( {{curl}\mathbf{F}} \right)\left( P_{0} \right)$$ for all points $$P$$ on $$S_{a}$$ because $${curl}\mathbf{F}$$ is continuous. Thus, by Stokes’ Theorem, we get the following approximation to the circulation around the boundary circle $$C_{a}$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{C_{a}}\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{S_{a}}{{curl}\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S_{a}}{{curl}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}dS}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{C_{a}}\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r}} \approx {\iint\limits_{S_{a}}{{curl}\mathbf{v}\left( P_{0} \right) \cdot \mathbf{n}\left( P_{0} \right)dS = {curl}\mathbf{v}\left( P_{0} \right) \cdot \mathbf{n}\left( P_{0} \right)\pi a^{2}}}} \end{array}$$
This approximation becomes better as $$\left. a\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ and we have
$${curl}\mathbf{v}\left( P_{0} \right) \cdot \mathbf{n}\left( P_{0} \right) = \underset{a\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{1}{\pi a^{2}}{\int_{C_{a}}{\mathbf{v} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}}$$

Equation 4 gives the relationship between the curl and the circulation. It shows that $${curl}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}$$ is a measure of the rotating effect of the fluid about the axis $$\mathbf{n}$$ . The curling effect is greatest about the axis parallel to $${curl}\mathbf{v}$$ .
Imagine a tiny paddle wheel placed in the fluid at a point $$P$$ , as in Figure 7; the paddle wheel rotates fastest when its axis is parallel to $${curl}\mathbf{v}$$ .

image.alt: Details An illustration of a paddle wheel is displayed. The paddle wheel has two rods intersecting at their midpoints, perpendicular to each other. At each end of the rods, a rectangular paddle is attached. Eight curved arrows are drawn around the paddles. The first four connect each paddle to the immediate next one and point counterclockwise. The remaining four are concentric to the first four, placed between and slightly away from the gap between the paddles, and also point counterclockwise. A vector, labeled curl vector v, rises from the intersection of the rods and slopes upward to the right, perpendicular to the plane of the curved arrows.

section.paragraph: Finally, we mention that Stokes’ Theorem can be used to prove Theorem 16.5.4 (which states that if $${curl}\mathbf{F} = 0$$ on all of $${\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ , then $$\mathbf{F}$$ is conservative). From our previous work (Theorems 16.3.3 and 16.3.4), we know that $$\mathbf{F}$$ is conservative if $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0}$$ for every closed path $$C$$ . Given $$C$$ , suppose we can find an orientable surface $$S$$ whose boundary is $$C$$ . (This can be done, but the proof requires advanced techniques.) Then Stokes’ Theorem gives
$$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = {\iint\limits_{S}{{curl}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = {\iint\limits_{S}{0 \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0}}}}}$$

A curve that is not simple can be broken into a number of simple curves, and the integrals around these simple curves are all $$0$$ . Adding these integrals, we obtain $$\int_{C}{\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0}$$ for any closed curve $$C$$ .

note.title: George Stokes
note.heading: George Stokes
note.paragraph: Stokes’ Theorem is named after the Irish mathematical physicist Sir George Stokes (1819–1903). Stokes was a professor at Cambridge University (in fact he held the same position as Newton, Lucasian Professor of Mathematics) and was especially noted for his studies of fluid flow and light. What we call Stokes’ Theorem was actually discovered by the Scottish physicist Sir William Thomson (1824–1907, known as Lord Kelvin). Stokes learned of this theorem in a letter from Thomson in 1850 and asked students to prove it on an examination at Cambridge University in 1854. We don’t know if any of those students was able to do so.
